meeting.text:
TRANSCRIPT: Riverbend Outdoor Co. planning meeting, spring catalog launch

Attendees: Dana (marketing lead), Marcus (operations), Lena (product), Theo (finance), Aiko (customer support)

Dana: Okay, let's get started. The goal today is to lock the plan for the spring catalog launch. We've been talking about it for three weeks, so I'd like decisions and owners by the end of this hour. First item, launch date. We floated March 3 and March 17.

Marcus: From the warehouse side, March 3 is tight. The new tent line, the Ridgeline 2 and Ridgeline 4, arrives from the supplier on February 20, and we need about ten working days to receive, inspect and shelve it. If anything is late, March 3 slips anyway.

Lena: And I still need final photos of the Ridgeline 4 in the fly-only configuration. The photographer can do February 24.

Theo: Finance doesn't mind either date, but if we launch on the 17th, the catalog revenue lands in Q1 either way, so there's no quarter-end pressure.

Dana: Then let's go with March 17. Any objections? No? Good. Decision: launch on March 17. Marcus, you own the receiving schedule.

Marcus: Got it. I'll send a receiving plan by Friday.

Dana: Second item, the print run. Last year we printed 40,000 catalogs and had about 6,000 left over. Theo, what did you model?

Theo: I modeled three options. 30,000 copies costs $1.42 each, so about $42,600. 35,000 drops to $1.31 each, about $45,850. And 40,000 is $1.24 each, about $49,600. Postage is separate and runs about 58 cents per catalog for the bulk rate. Response rate on printed catalogs last spring was 2.1 percent, with an average order of $118.

Dana: So the extra 5,000 from 30 to 35 costs about $3,250 plus postage.

Theo: Right, roughly $6,150 all in for the extra 5,000. At a 2.1 percent response rate and $118 average order, those 5,000 would bring in around $12,400 in orders, but the newer names on the list historically respond at about half the rate.

Lena: The new list segment is mostly people who signed up at the fall trade shows. They're engaged but they haven't bought yet.

Dana: Let's go with 35,000 and send the extra to the trade-show segment, but let's track that segment separately so we know next year. Theo, can you set up the tracking codes?

Theo: Yes. I'll use a separate promo code on those 5,000, something like RIVER35.

Dana: Decision: 35,000 copies, trade-show segment tracked with its own code. Theo owns it. Third item, pricing on the Ridgeline line. Lena?

Lena: The Ridgeline 2 was planned at $279 and the Ridgeline 4 at $389. Our closest competitor dropped their four-person tent to $369 last month. I'd like to hold $389 because ours has the full-coverage fly and the vestibule on both doors, but I know that's a debate.

Theo: Margin on the Ridgeline 4 at $389 is 46 percent. At $369 it'd be 43 percent. Either is above our 40 percent floor.

Aiko: Can I add something from support? The most common complaint on the old four-person tent was that the poles were hard to set up alone. If the Ridgeline 4 fixes that, we should say it loudly.

Lena: It does. The color-coded clips and the hub pole. One person can pitch it in about eight minutes.

Dana: Then I'm with Lena. Hold $389 and lead with the solo setup in the copy. We can run a launch promotion instead of cutting the price. Ten percent off for the first two weeks for loyalty members?

Theo: Ten percent for two weeks is fine. I'd cap it at one tent per order.

Dana: Decision: Ridgeline 2 at $279, Ridgeline 4 at $389, ten percent off for loyalty members for the first two weeks, one per order. Lena owns the copy, and she'll get the eight-minute setup claim checked.

Lena: I'll time five people who have never pitched it. If the median is over ten minutes we change the claim.

Dana: Good. Fourth item, support readiness. Aiko?

Aiko: Last spring we had a spike of about 1,800 tickets in the first week, mostly order status and sizing. We had four people on support and the average first response time went to 31 hours. I'd like two temporary agents for the first three weeks, and a sizing guide on every product page.

Theo: Two temps for three weeks is about $7,800 through the agency.

Dana: Approved. Can we also add a setup video for the Ridgeline tents? That should cut tickets.

Aiko: Yes, that would help a lot. Can the video be under two minutes?

Lena: I'll make sure it is. We can film it the same day as the photos, February 24.

Dana: Decision: two temporary agents for three weeks, a sizing guide on product pages, and a setup video under two minutes filmed on February 24. Aiko owns staffing, Lena owns the video.

Marcus: One risk I want on the record. The supplier said there's a chance the Ridgeline 4 fly arrives a week after the tent bodies. If that happens, we can't ship complete tents until it does.

Dana: What's the fallback?

Marcus: We could launch with the Ridgeline 2 in stock and take pre-orders on the Ridgeline 4, shipping by March 31.

Dana: Then that's the fallback. If the fly is late, Ridgeline 4 goes to pre-order with a ship-by date of March 31, and support gets a script. Marcus will confirm with the supplier by February 10 whether the fly is on time.

Aiko: I'll draft the pre-order script either way so we're ready.

Dana: Last item, the email schedule. Three emails: a teaser on March 10, launch on March 17, and a last-chance reminder for the loyalty discount on March 29. Any conflicts?

Theo: March 29 is right before the promo ends on the 31st, that works.

Dana: Good. Let's recap the owners. Marcus: receiving plan by Friday and supplier confirmation by February 10. Theo: tracking code for the trade-show segment. Lena: copy, the setup-time test, and the video. Aiko: temporary agents, sizing guide, and the pre-order script. I'll own the email schedule and the overall timeline. We'll meet again on February 12 to check progress. Thanks, everyone.

Dana: Before we go, one more thing that came up in the chat. Theo, you mentioned the shipping rates.

Theo: Right. Our carrier is raising ground shipping rates by 6.9 percent on February 1. Our free-shipping threshold is $75 today. If we keep it, shipping costs as a share of revenue go from about 7.2 percent to 7.7 percent. If we raise the threshold to $89, my model says about 30 percent of orders between $75 and $89 add something to reach the new threshold, and shipping cost stays around 7.2 percent.

Lena: Raising it right before the launch feels bad. The Ridgeline 2 is $279, so tent buyers clear either threshold. It's the accessory buyers who'd notice.

Aiko: Support would hear about it. Last time we changed the threshold, we got about 200 tickets in a week asking about it.

Dana: Let's not change it before the launch. We'll revisit in April with the launch data. Theo, can you bring the numbers to the April review?

Theo: Sure. I'll also look at a flat $5.95 shipping option for orders under $75, which some competitors do.

Dana: Decision: keep the $75 free-shipping threshold through the spring launch, revisit in April. Theo owns the analysis. Anything else?

Marcus: Just that the warehouse will be closed on February 17 for the inventory count. Orders placed that day ship on the 18th.

Aiko: I'll add that to the support macros.

Dana: Good. And Lena, the loyalty email list, how many people are on it now?

Lena: About 48,000 active loyalty members, up from 39,000 last spring. Roughly a third of them bought camping gear in the last year.

Dana: So the ten percent loyalty promotion could reach around 16,000 recent campers. That's a good audience. Let's make sure the teaser email goes to them first, a day before the general list. So the loyalty teaser goes March 9 and the general teaser March 10.

Theo: That works for the promo codes, I'll make the loyalty code active on the 17th for everyone at once.

Dana: Decision: loyalty members get the teaser on March 9, the general list on March 10, and the loyalty discount code activates on March 17. Lena, please update the email calendar. Last call, anything else? Then we're done. Thanks, everyone, see you on February 12.

Action item summary (sent after the meeting by Dana):
- Launch date: March 17.
- Print run: 35,000 catalogs; trade-show segment tracked with code RIVER35 (Theo).
- Pricing: Ridgeline 2 $279, Ridgeline 4 $389; loyalty members 10 percent off for two weeks, one tent per order.
- Setup claim: test with five first-time pitchers; change the claim if the median is over ten minutes (Lena).
- Support: two temporary agents for three weeks, sizing guide, setup video under two minutes (Aiko, Lena).
- Risk: if the Ridgeline 4 fly is late, pre-orders with ship-by March 31 (Marcus confirms by February 10).
- Shipping threshold stays $75 through launch; review in April (Theo).
- Email schedule: loyalty teaser March 9, general teaser March 10, launch March 17, last chance March 29.
- Next check-in: February 12.


TRANSCRIPT: Operations breakout, same afternoon (follow-on session)

Attendees: Dana (marketing lead), Marcus (operations), Theo (finance), Aiko (customer support). Lena sent her regrets; she was at the photo studio scouting for the February shoot.

Dana: Thanks for staying on. This is the session for the things we didn't have time for this morning. Nothing here changes the launch decisions; it's the operational stuff around them. I have four topics: returns, warehouse staffing, packaging, and the fall trade shows. Marcus, you wanted returns first.

Marcus: Yes. Tent returns are a different animal from jackets. Last season, about 8 percent of tents came back, and more than half of those had been pitched at least once. Some came back muddy, one came back with a burned vestibule. Right now our policy says unused items within 60 days, and used items only if defective. Customer support ends up making exceptions all the time.

Aiko: We do. If someone says it leaked on the first night, we take it back. The trouble is we can't tell a leak from a person who pitched it in a ditch. Agents spend a lot of time going back and forth with photos.

Theo: What does a returned used tent cost us?

Marcus: We inspect it, and if it's clean and intact we sell it as "lightly used" through the outlet page at about 60 percent of full price. If it needs cleaning, that's about $22 in labor. If the fly or floor is damaged, we usually can't resell it at all, and it goes to the donation partner.

Theo: So a used return that's clean costs us about 40 percent of the price, and a damaged one costs us all of it.

Dana: What would you change?

Marcus: Two things. A clear "trail tested" promise, which is that you can pitch it, sleep in it, and return it within 30 days if it doesn't work for you, as long as it's clean and dry. And a short checklist on the return form, so customers tell us up front whether it was used and whether anything is damaged.

Aiko: I like the checklist. It would save my team the photo exchange in most cases. I'd also want a "send us a photo of the seam" step for leak claims, so the warranty team can tell manufacturing defects from wear.

Theo: My worry with a 30-day trail-tested promise is abuse. People take it on one trip and send it back.

Marcus: Some will. But competitors already offer it, and the number of returns didn't jump when they started, according to the trade association survey. I'd rather pilot it.

Dana: Then let's pilot it on the Ridgeline line only, for the spring season, and measure it. Marcus, can you write up the terms for review?

Marcus: I'll have a draft in two weeks.

Dana: Decision, tentatively: a 30-day trail-tested return pilot on the Ridgeline line, clean and dry, with a return checklist. Marcus drafts the terms; we review at the next check-in. Theo, please set up a way to track return cost by reason.

Theo: Will do. I'll split it into unused, clean used, needs cleaning, and damaged.

Dana: Second topic, warehouse staffing.

Marcus: We have eleven full-time people in the warehouse. During the spring peak last year we added six seasonal pickers from the staffing agency, starting the second week of March. Orders per day peaked at about 2,300, and our pick-pack time crept from one day to three days for about a week. That's where a lot of the order status tickets came from.

Aiko: That week was rough. Most of our "where is my order" tickets were from people whose orders hadn't left the building.

Marcus: This year I'd like eight seasonal pickers, starting a week earlier, and I want to run a Saturday shift for the first three weekends after launch. The agency rate is about $24 an hour, plus their fee.

Theo: Ballpark?

Marcus: Eight people for six weeks at 40 hours is about $46,000 with the agency fee. The Saturday shifts add about $6,000.

Theo: That's more than last year, but if it keeps pick-pack at one day, it pays for itself in fewer tickets and fewer cancellations. I'm fine with it, as long as we can end the contract early if volume is lower than forecast.

Marcus: The agency allows one week's notice.

Dana: Approved. Marcus owns it. Aiko, can you tell us when the order-status ticket share drops below the normal level, so we know when to release the seasonal staff?

Aiko: Yes. Normally order status is about 25 percent of tickets. I'll send a daily number during launch.

Dana: Third topic, packaging. We keep getting comments about the plastic.

Marcus: Right now tents ship in a printed plastic bag inside a brown box, with plastic air pillows. The supplier can switch the inner bag to a paper sleeve for about 14 cents more per unit. Air pillows could be replaced with paper fill. The paper fill is heavier, which adds a little shipping cost on the lighter items.

Theo: How much heavier?

Marcus: About 90 grams per box on average. For most orders it doesn't change the shipping tier at all. For a few small accessory orders, it bumps them up a tier.

Aiko: Customers notice this. We get maybe 30 messages a month about the plastic, and those people are often our most loyal customers.

Dana: Can we do it in time for the launch?

Marcus: The paper sleeves, no. The supplier needs ten weeks of lead time, so that would be for the summer orders. The paper fill, yes. I can switch the warehouse over in two weeks once the current stock of pillows runs out.

Dana: Then let's do the paper fill now and the paper sleeves for summer orders. Theo, please watch the shipping cost on small orders and tell us if it moves.

Theo: I'll add it to the April shipping review. That's the same analysis we already planned.

Dana: Decision: switch to paper fill now, paper sleeves for summer, Marcus owns it, Theo watches shipping cost. Last topic, fall trade shows. Theo, you had numbers.

Theo: Last fall we went to three shows. The booth cost was about $9,000 per show, plus travel for three people and shipping the display. All in, about $41,000. We collected roughly 5,000 sign-ups across the three shows, which is the segment we're mailing extra catalogs to. Until that tracking comes back, we don't know what those sign-ups are worth.

Dana: So the trade-show decision depends on the spring results.

Theo: Exactly. Booth deposits for the fall shows are due in May, so if we wait for the spring numbers we'd have about six weeks of data. That's thin, but it's something.

Marcus: From the operations side, the display we built two years ago is getting worn. If we go again, it needs about $3,500 of repairs or a new one.

Aiko: Can I make a pitch for one of the shows? The regional outdoor expo is where we meet a lot of existing customers, not just new ones. People come to the booth with their old tents and ask questions. It's the best customer feedback we get all year.

Dana: That's a good point. Let's not decide today. Theo, please bring the spring tracking numbers to a short meeting in mid-May, and we'll decide how many shows to do then. Marcus, please get a quote for repairing the display, just so we have it.

Marcus: Okay.

Dana: Let me recap this session, since it's separate from this morning's list. Marcus: draft the trail-tested return terms in two weeks, book eight seasonal pickers and the Saturday shifts, switch to paper fill, and get a quote for the display repair. Theo: track return cost by reason, watch small-order shipping cost, and bring trade-show tracking numbers in mid-May. Aiko: daily order-status ticket share during launch. I'll send this to the whole team, including Lena, so everyone is on the same page.

Aiko: One more small thing. The support phone hours. We close at 6 p.m. on weekdays and we're closed on weekends. Last spring a lot of people tried to reach us on the first Saturday after launch.

Dana: Could we open on Saturdays for the first three weekends, to match the warehouse shift?

Aiko: With the two temps, yes. I'd do 9 to 1 on Saturdays, chat and messages only, no phone.

Theo: That doesn't add cost if it's within the temps' hours.

Dana: Then let's do it. Decision: Saturday chat and messages from 9 to 1 for the first three weekends after launch. Aiko owns it. Okay, that's everything. Thanks for staying late.

Breakout action items (sent by Dana to the full team):
- Returns: 30-day trail-tested return pilot on the Ridgeline line, clean and dry, with a return checklist; Marcus drafts terms in two weeks; Theo tracks return cost by reason.
- Warehouse: eight seasonal pickers starting a week earlier than last year, plus Saturday shifts for the first three weekends after launch; can end early with one week's notice (Marcus).
- Packaging: paper fill now, paper sleeves for summer orders (Marcus); small-order shipping cost added to the April review (Theo).
- Trade shows: decision deferred to a mid-May meeting with spring tracking numbers (Theo); display repair quote (Marcus).
- Support: Saturday chat and messages, 9 to 1, for the first three weekends after launch; daily order-status ticket share during launch (Aiko).

Notes Aiko added to the shared document after the breakout, for context:

Last spring's launch tickets, first three weeks, by category: order status 34 percent; sizing and fit 21 percent; returns and exchanges 14 percent; setup questions 11 percent; promo code problems 8 percent; damaged in transit 5 percent; everything else 7 percent. Most promo code problems were customers who typed the code with a space at the end, so the checkout now trims spaces automatically. Most damaged-in-transit tickets were stove fuel canisters that leaked in the box, which is why the warehouse now bags them separately.

Average first response time by channel last spring: chat about 4 minutes during open hours, messages about 9 hours, email 31 hours at the worst point. The email number is the one that hurt our reviews. With two temps, I'm aiming for under 12 hours on email during the launch weeks and under 2 hours on messages during Saturday coverage.

Macros we need before launch, besides the pre-order script: the warehouse closure on February 17, the paper fill change (people will ask whether it's recyclable; it is, in curbside paper recycling), the trail-tested return pilot once Marcus's terms are approved, and the Saturday hours. I'll circulate drafts to Dana and Marcus a week before launch.

Marcus's note on receiving, added the same evening: the receiving dock can unload two containers a day. The Ridgeline shipment is three containers, so receiving takes at least two days before inspection starts. Inspection is a sample of one tent in twenty, fully pitched in the warehouse, checking poles, clips, seams and the zipper on both doors. Any carton with a failed sample gets a full count. The inspection crew is the same four people who do the inventory count, which is another reason the count can't move off February 17.

Theo's note on budget, also added after the meeting: the breakout decisions together add about $55,000 to the spring operating budget, mostly the seasonal pickers. The packaging change adds about $0.14 per tent from summer onward, and an estimated $1,100 a month in paper fill over what we spend on air pillows. All of this is within the contingency line we set aside in January, so no separate approval is needed.

prd.title: Bike-share app requirements
prd.text:
PRODUCT REQUIREMENTS: Pedal Pass, the bike-share app redesign (version 3.0)

Background. Pedal Pass runs 2,400 bikes across 310 docking stations in the metro area. The current app (version 2.6) has a 3.1-star rating. The top three complaints in app reviews over the last six months are: unlocking takes too long or fails (38 percent of negative reviews), it's hard to find a dock with free space at the end of a ride (27 percent), and confusing pricing (19 percent). Ride volume is 41,000 rides per week in summer and about 15,000 per week in winter. 62 percent of riders are on a monthly membership; the rest pay per ride.

Goals for 3.0. First, cut median time from opening the app to an unlocked bike from 48 seconds to under 15 seconds. Second, reduce rides that end with the rider unable to dock at their first-choice station by half. Third, raise the app rating to at least 4.2 stars within six months of launch. A non-goal for this release is adding e-scooters, which is planned for a later version.

Requirement 1: Quick unlock. When the app opens within 50 meters of a station, it shows a single large Unlock button for the nearest available bike, with the bike number. Tapping it unlocks the bike without scanning a code. If Bluetooth is off, the app falls back to scanning the QR code on the handlebar. Unlock must succeed or show a clear error within 5 seconds. If unlock fails twice, the app offers the next nearest bike. The target is that 95 percent of unlocks complete in under 10 seconds from tapping the button.

Requirement 2: Dock availability while riding. During a ride, the app shows the three stations nearest to the rider's destination with the number of free docks, refreshed every 30 seconds. If the chosen station drops to two or fewer free docks, the app sends a notification suggesting the next best station. Riders who end at a suggested alternative station because their first choice was full get ten free minutes added to their account, up to twice per week.

Requirement 3: Clear pricing. Before unlocking, the app shows the price in plain words, for example "$1 to unlock, then 25 cents a minute" for pay-per-ride, or "Included in your membership for the first 45 minutes" for members. The current pricing stays the same: pay-per-ride riders pay $1 to unlock plus 25 cents per minute; members get 45 minutes per ride included and pay 15 cents per minute after that; the monthly membership costs $19. During a ride, the app shows the running cost. After the ride, the receipt shows the duration, the cost, and any credits applied.

Requirement 4: Ride history and receipts. Riders can see their last 12 months of rides, with route maps, and can export a month of receipts as a PDF for expense reports. Corporate members can add a cost-center code to each ride.

Requirement 5: Accessibility. All screens support Dynamic Type up to the largest accessibility size and work with VoiceOver. The Unlock button must be at least 60 points tall. Color is never the only way to show dock availability; numbers are always shown.

Requirement 6: Offline behavior. If the phone loses its connection during a ride, the ride continues and the app shows the last known dock counts with a note that they may be out of date. The ride ends normally when the bike is docked, and the app syncs when the connection returns.

Requirement 7: Reporting a problem. From the ride screen, riders can report a problem with the bike in two taps: flat tire, brakes, chain, seat, or other. A reported bike is locked out of rentals until a technician checks it. Riders who report a problem in the first two minutes of a ride are not charged for the ride.

Success metrics. We will measure median time to unlock, the share of rides that end at a station other than the rider's first choice because it was full, the app rating, weekly active riders, and support tickets about unlocking. The support team currently receives about 900 unlocking tickets per month; the target is under 300.

Rollout plan. Version 3.0 goes to 5 percent of riders for two weeks, then 25 percent for one week, then everyone. We will roll back if the unlock failure rate rises above 3 percent or if crash-free sessions fall below 99.5 percent. The planned start of the 5 percent rollout is April 14, timed before the summer peak.

Open questions. Should members be able to reserve a bike for up to 10 minutes before they reach the station? Product favors it; operations worries it will leave bikes idle at busy stations during the morning peak. Should the ten free minutes for docking at an alternative station also apply to pay-per-ride riders? Finance estimates that credit costs about $4,000 per month in summer if applied to everyone. Should we show a carbon savings estimate after each ride? Design likes it; some riders found it preachy in a survey.

Dependencies. The quick unlock depends on the new Bluetooth locks, installed on 1,900 of the 2,400 bikes so far; the remaining 500 will be fitted by the end of March. Dock counts depend on the station API, which currently refreshes every 60 seconds and needs to support 30 seconds. The PDF export depends on the billing team's new receipt service.

Team. Product manager: Ines Calder. Engineering lead: Rafael Moretti. Design lead: Sun-hee Park. Operations: Grant Whitfield. The weekly status review is on Tuesdays.

Appendix A: Research findings. We interviewed 24 riders in December: 12 members, 8 pay-per-ride riders and 4 people who had stopped riding. The most common story was arriving at a station during the morning rush to find no free docks and riding 6 to 10 minutes to the next one while the meter ran. Three riders said they had stopped using Pedal Pass for commuting for that reason alone. Members said they liked the membership price but did not understand when the 45 included minutes reset; several thought it was 45 minutes per day rather than per ride. Pay-per-ride riders most often said they could not tell what a ride had cost until the receipt arrived. Riders who use VoiceOver said the current map is unusable because stations are announced only as "pin." Two riders asked for a way to save favorite stations, such as home and work.

Appendix B: Unlock failure analysis. In the last 90 days, 7.8 percent of unlock attempts failed on the first try. Of the failures, 54 percent were QR scans that took more than 20 seconds or did not read, usually in low light; 29 percent were network timeouts when the server took too long to confirm the bike; and 17 percent were bikes that had a fault but had not been reported. Bikes with the new Bluetooth locks failed on the first try 2.1 percent of the time, compared with 9.4 percent for the old cellular locks. The quick unlock in Requirement 1 should therefore be enabled only for bikes with the new locks, and the app should prefer suggesting those bikes when both kinds are available at a station.

Appendix C: Favorite stations (proposed for 3.1). Riders can mark up to five stations as favorites. The home screen then shows free bikes and free docks at each favorite. This is out of scope for 3.0 but the data model in 3.0 should allow it, so the station list must support a per-user favorites flag.

Appendix D: Analytics events. The app logs these events with timestamps and no personal information beyond the rider's account ID: app_open, unlock_tap, unlock_success, unlock_failure (with reason), ride_start, dock_suggestion_shown, dock_suggestion_accepted, ride_end, problem_reported, and receipt_exported. Location is logged only at ride start and ride end, rounded to the nearest station.

Appendix E: Launch communications. Members get an email two days before their phone receives the update, describing quick unlock and dock suggestions. In-app, the first launch of 3.0 shows three short cards, which riders can skip: quick unlock, dock suggestions, and the new pricing display. Station signs are not changing in this release.

Appendix F: Support readiness. Support will receive a one-hour training session the week before the 5 percent rollout, plus a one-page guide to common problems: what to do when quick unlock is unavailable for a bike with an old lock, how to apply docking credits manually, and how to export receipts for riders whose app is out of date. Support will tag tickets with "3.0" during the rollout so the team can compare ticket volume between riders on the new and old versions.


Appendix G: Notifications. Version 3.0 sends only three kinds of push notification, and riders can turn each one off separately in Settings. Dock alerts: the low-dock notification described in Requirement 2, sent at most twice per ride and never in the last 200 meters before the station, when the rider is already committed. Ride reminders: a notification when a ride has lasted 40 minutes, so members know their included time is nearly used, and a second one if a ride passes two hours, in case the rider forgot to dock. Account notices: a failed payment, an expiring card, or a membership renewal. Marketing notifications are not part of this release. Notification permission is requested after the rider's first completed ride, not at first launch, because the research in Appendix A showed riders decline permission prompts that appear before they understand why the app needs them. If a rider declines, the dock alert still appears as a banner inside the app while the app is open on the ride screen.

Appendix H: Account, sign-in and payment. Riders sign in with Sign in with Apple, Google, or an emailed one-time code; passwords are being retired, and existing password accounts are asked to switch the first time they open 3.0. Saved payment methods are Apple Pay, Google Pay and cards stored with the payment processor; the app never stores full card numbers on the device or on our servers. A rider can have only one active ride at a time on an account. Group rides, where one account unlocks up to three bikes for friends, are planned for a later version and should not be blocked by any 3.0 data model decision. Corporate members sign in with their work account through the existing single sign-on integration, which does not change in 3.0.

Appendix I: Station API changes. The station API serves dock counts, bike counts and bike types for every station. To support the 30-second refresh, the API team will move dock counts from a database query on each request to a cache updated by the stations themselves, which already report every 15 seconds over the cellular network. The cache answers a request for all 310 stations in under 100 milliseconds. Stations that have not reported for more than three minutes are marked as "status unknown" in the app, shown in gray with the last known numbers and the time of the last report, rather than being hidden. The API will also add a field for whether each bike has the new Bluetooth lock, which the quick unlock and the bike suggestion logic both need. Load testing will simulate the summer peak, which is roughly 4,000 riders with the app open at the same time, each refreshing every 30 seconds, plus a safety margin of three times that load.

Appendix J: Station map. The map shows stations as circles with the number of free bikes inside before a ride, and the number of free docks inside during a ride, so the same screen answers the question the rider has at that moment. Stations with zero bikes or zero docks show a zero and an outlined circle, never just a color. The map clusters stations when zoomed out and shows individual stations at street level. Tapping a station opens a card with the station name, counts by bike type, walking distance, and a button to get walking or riding directions in the rider's preferred maps app. For VoiceOver users, each station is announced by name, distance and counts, for example "Harbor and Fifth, 120 meters, 6 bikes, 4 docks", and the list view described below is offered as an alternative to the map.

Appendix K: List view. Every map screen has a list view that shows the same stations sorted by distance. The list is the default for VoiceOver users and for anyone who chooses it in Settings. Each row shows the station name, distance, bike and dock counts, and a small note if the station's status is unknown. Riders can pull to refresh, but the list also refreshes on the normal schedule.

Appendix L: Edge cases. The following cases need defined behavior and test coverage. A bike is pushed into a dock but the lock does not engage: the app keeps the ride running, shows "Not docked yet, push the bike in until the light turns green," and offers to report a dock problem after 60 seconds. A rider docks at a station that has lost its network connection: the dock records the end time locally and the ride is closed when the station reconnects, using the recorded time, not the reconnection time. The rider's phone dies during a ride: the ride ends normally when the bike is docked, and the receipt is waiting when the phone is back on. A bike is left undocked: after two hours the app sends the reminder in Appendix G, and after twelve hours support contacts the rider. A rider tries to unlock while a previous ride has not been closed: the app shows the open ride with an option to report that the bike was docked, which support reviews within one business day. A station is removed or relocated: riders with that station saved in recent searches see "This station has moved" with the nearest replacement.

Appendix M: Localization. Version 3.0 ships in English and Spanish, which together cover more than 95 percent of riders according to the device language data. All strings must be in the localization files from the start, with no text in images. Prices use the rider's locale for formatting but are always in US dollars. Station names are not translated. Vietnamese and Chinese are planned for 3.1, depending on demand from the community partners program.

Appendix N: Quality and testing. Quick unlock will be tested on the 15 phone models that account for 90 percent of rides, including at least three phones more than four years old, since older Bluetooth chips were the most common cause of slow pairing in the lock vendor's field tests. Each model is tested at three stations chosen for difficult conditions: an underground transit hub with weak cellular signal, a waterfront station with heavy Bluetooth interference from nearby venues, and a busy downtown station with more than 30 docks. The test plan also covers the fallback to QR scanning, offline rides, Dynamic Type at every size, VoiceOver on every screen, and the Spanish strings. A beta group of 300 volunteer riders will use builds through TestFlight and the Play Store testing track for the four weeks before the 5 percent rollout. Volunteers get one free month of membership as thanks.

Appendix O: Privacy review. The privacy review covers the analytics events in Appendix D and the location handling during rides. The app requests location permission "while using the app" only, never "always." Ride routes for the history map in Requirement 4 are stored for 12 months and then deleted; riders can delete any single ride's route sooner from the ride history screen, which keeps the receipt but removes the map. Route data is never sold or shared with advertisers. Aggregated, anonymous trip counts between stations may be shared with the city transportation department under the existing data-sharing agreement, which requires at least 10 trips before any station pair is reported.

Appendix P: Out of scope for 3.0. To protect the timeline, the following are explicitly out of scope: e-scooters (see the Goals section), group rides, bike reservations (pending the open question above), favorite stations (Appendix C), a widget or watch app, Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, in-app chat with support, gift memberships, and a redesign of the website. Requests for these during the project should be logged in the backlog and reviewed for 3.1.

Appendix Q: Glossary. Dock: a single parking slot that locks a bike. Station: a group of docks at one location. Quick unlock: unlocking the nearest bike with one tap over Bluetooth, described in Requirement 1. First-choice station: the station the rider selected as the destination when starting the ride, or the station nearest the destination entered in the app. Alternative station: any station suggested by the app after the first-choice station dropped to two or fewer free docks. Crash-free session: an app session that ends without the app crashing, as measured by the crash reporting service. Old locks: the cellular locks installed before the Bluetooth upgrade.

Appendix R: Decision log. In January the team decided to keep the QR fallback for all bikes rather than remove it, because about 6 percent of riders have Bluetooth turned off and some riders borrow phones without the app's permissions granted. The team also decided not to show the carbon estimate on the receipt in 3.0 while the open question is unresolved, but to keep the calculation in the backend so it can be turned on without an app release. In February the team decided to require the latest two major phone operating system versions, which drops support for about 4 percent of current riders; those riders will keep the 2.6 app, which will continue to work until the end of the year, and will be told in the app that they need to update their phone to get the new features.

Appendix S: Ride screen layout. The ride screen is the screen riders see most, and it must be readable at a glance on a handlebar mount. From top to bottom it shows: the elapsed time in large numbers; the running cost, or the included minutes remaining for members; the destination station with its free dock count; the two alternative stations in a smaller row; and a bottom bar with the report-a-problem button and an end-of-ride help button. The screen stays awake during a ride if the phone is on a mount and charging, and dims after one minute otherwise. In dark mode, the dock counts keep the same contrast ratio as in light mode. Nothing on the ride screen requires a precise tap while riding; the smallest target is 44 points, and the alternative stations can be chosen by swiping the destination card.

Appendix T: Operations impact. The dock suggestions in Requirement 2 will shift some rides from full stations to nearby ones, which changes where bikes pile up. Operations runs four rebalancing vans that move bikes from full stations to empty ones, mostly during the morning and evening peaks. Operations has asked for a daily report of accepted dock suggestions by station, so the van routes can be adjusted after the first month. The bike problem reports in Requirement 7 go into the same maintenance queue technicians use today, with the rider's category and the bike number; a photo option was considered and dropped for 3.0 because the two-tap goal matters more. Technicians clear a reported bike in the app they already use, which unlocks it for rentals again.

Appendix U: Support ticket categories. To measure the success metric for unlocking tickets consistently, support will use these categories from the start of the beta: unlock failed, unlock slow, wrong bike unlocked, ride did not end, charged incorrectly, docking credit missing, receipt or export problem, account or sign-in, bike problem, and other. The current ticket system lumps the first three together as "unlock"; the team will map historical tickets to the new categories by keyword so the before-and-after comparison is fair.

Appendix V: Milestones. Design for all screens in this document is complete by the end of January. The station API cache and the Bluetooth lock field are complete by mid-February, so the app team can build against the real API. Feature complete for the app is March 7. The beta described in Appendix N runs for the four weeks before the rollout. The support training and guide in Appendix F happen in the week before the rollout. The rollout itself follows the plan in the Rollout section. Each milestone is reviewed at the weekly status review, and any milestone that slips by more than one week is raised with the product and engineering directors the same day.

Appendix W: Riders who stopped riding. Four of the 24 research participants had stopped riding. Their reasons were, in order: no dock at the end of the commute, the cost of rides that ran long because of detours to find a dock, a slow unlock that made them miss a train, and moving to a neighborhood without stations. The first three are addressed by Requirements 1 through 3. The team will email a sample of riders who have not ridden in the last six months when 3.0 is fully rolled out, describing the changes and offering a free ride credit, and will measure how many come back within 30 days.

Appendix X: Accessibility review. An outside accessibility consultant will review the beta build, including the quick unlock flow, the ride screen, the station map and list view, receipts, and the Spanish strings, with VoiceOver, TalkBack, Switch Control and the largest Dynamic Type size. Any issue the consultant rates as blocking must be fixed before the 25 percent stage. The consultant will also test the app with two riders who are blind or have low vision, recruited through the community partners program, and both riders will be paid for their time.

Appendix Y: Competitive review. The design team reviewed five bike-share and scooter apps in other cities. The fastest unlock among them took about 9 seconds from opening the app, using a similar one-button Bluetooth flow; the slowest took more than a minute and required scanning a code and confirming a payment screen. Two of the five show dock availability during a ride, and only one suggests an alternative station automatically. None of them shows a running cost during the ride in a way the design team judged clear; most show only elapsed time. Three of the five have a list view for screen-reader users, and one was rated highly by a disability advocacy group for its station announcements, which inspired the format in Appendix J. Riders in our research who had used other cities' systems most often mentioned the one-button unlock as the feature they wished Pedal Pass had.

Appendix Z: Frequently asked questions from the internal review. Will the quick unlock drain riders' batteries? No; Bluetooth scanning runs only while the app is open within 50 meters of a station, and stops as soon as a bike is unlocked. Will station sign-ups or membership sales change in this release? No; the membership signup flow is unchanged apart from the new pricing wording. Can a rider still unlock a bike with the old card-tap readers at stations? Yes; station kiosks and member cards are unaffected by this release. What happens to rides started in the 2.6 app when a rider updates during a ride? The ride continues and appears in 3.0 when the update finishes; the update is not offered while a ride is active. Will the website show the new dock counts? The website already uses the station API, so it gets the faster refresh automatically, but its design is not changing.

Document history. Draft 1 in November covered Requirements 1 through 3 only. Draft 2 in December added Requirements 4 through 7 and the research findings in Appendix A. Draft 3 in January added the unlock failure analysis, the analytics events, and the station API changes after the API team's estimate came back. This draft, version 4, adds the notification rules, the edge cases, localization, the testing and privacy plans, and the decision log, and it is the version the team will build from. Further changes need agreement at the weekly status review and are recorded in the decision log in Appendix R, with the date, the change, and the reason, so that anyone joining the project later can see why the product works the way it does. Comments on this draft are open until the end of the month; after that, the document is frozen for 3.0 and new ideas go to the 3.1 backlog described in Appendix P.

policy.title: Travel and expense policy
policy.text:
NORTHWIND LABS TRAVEL AND EXPENSE POLICY (effective January 1)

Purpose. This policy explains what business travel and expenses Northwind Labs pays for, how to book, and how to get reimbursed. It applies to all employees and contractors traveling on company business. When in doubt, ask your manager before you spend the money.

Approval. All travel needs your manager's approval in the travel tool before booking. International travel also needs approval from your department's vice president at least 21 days before departure. Trips to attend conferences need approval at least 30 days in advance so we can get early registration rates.

Booking flights. Book through the company travel tool so trips are covered by our travel insurance and duty-of-care program. Book at least 14 days before departure when possible. Economy class is the standard for all flights. Premium economy is allowed for flights with a scheduled flight time over 6 hours. Business class is allowed only for flights over 10 hours, and only with vice-president approval. You may keep frequent flyer miles, but you may not choose a more expensive flight to earn them. Checked bag fees are reimbursed for one bag on trips up to five days and two bags on longer trips. Seat selection fees up to $50 per flight are reimbursed.

Hotels. Book hotels through the travel tool. The nightly limit, before taxes, is $250 in most cities and $350 in high-cost cities, which are listed in the appendix and include New York, San Francisco, London, Zurich, and Tokyo. If you can't find a room under the limit, for example during a large conference, book the closest reasonable option and add a note explaining why. You may stay with friends or family instead of a hotel; in that case you may expense a thank-you gift of up to $75 per trip.

Ground transportation. Use public transit, shuttles, or ride-hailing when practical. Rental cars are allowed when they are cheaper than the alternatives or when you're traveling to several sites; book a midsize car or smaller. Decline the rental company's insurance in the United States, since our corporate policy covers it; accept it in other countries. If you drive your own car, we reimburse mileage at the current federal rate, plus parking and tolls, but not fuel, repairs or traffic tickets. Airport parking is reimbursed up to $30 per day.

Meals. When traveling, you may claim actual meal costs up to a daily limit of $85 in most cities and $110 in high-cost cities, including tips. Alcohol is reimbursed only at client meals and only in moderation; it is never reimbursed when eaten alone. Meals included in a conference fee or provided on a flight should not be claimed. For client meals, list the attendees and their company and the business purpose. Client meals over $150 per person need prior approval from your director.

Per diem option. Instead of claiming actual meal costs, employees traveling for more than five consecutive days may choose a flat per diem of $70 per day in most cities and $90 in high-cost cities, with no receipts required. You must choose either per diem or actual costs for the whole trip, not day by day.

Other reimbursable expenses. In-flight wifi on flights over 2 hours, hotel internet when not included, laundry on trips longer than five nights, work visas and passport photos for required business trips, and reasonable tips for hotel staff. Phone roaming plans for international trips are reimbursed up to $10 per day.

Non-reimbursable expenses. Personal entertainment, including movies and minibar items; upgrades you choose for comfort; spouse or family travel; fines and penalties; lost luggage or personal items; gym or spa fees; and travel insurance you buy yourself.

Combining business and personal travel. You may add personal days to a business trip, as long as the airfare is no more than $200 higher than the fare for the business dates alone. If it is more, you pay the difference. Hotel nights and meals on personal days are yours.

Receipts and deadlines. Submit expenses within 30 days of returning from a trip. Receipts are required for every expense of $25 or more, and for all hotel stays regardless of amount. Missing receipts need a signed explanation, and you may claim missing receipts no more than three times per calendar year. Expenses submitted more than 60 days after the trip will not be reimbursed, except with written approval from the chief financial officer.

Corporate card. Employees who travel more than four times per year should apply for a corporate card. The card may be used only for business expenses. You remain responsible for submitting the expense report; the card company is paid directly, but unreported charges will be deducted from your paycheck after 90 days.

Cancellations and changes. If a trip is canceled for business reasons, the company covers cancellation fees. If you cancel for personal reasons, you may be asked to cover fees above $100. Unused nonrefundable tickets should be recorded in the travel tool so the credit can be used on a later trip.

Safety. Register every international trip in the travel tool so the security team can reach you. If a destination has a travel advisory of level 3 or higher, you need approval from both your vice president and the security team.

Violations. Expenses that don't follow this policy may be rejected. Repeated or intentional violations may lead to disciplinary action, up to and including termination.

Appendix: Frequently asked questions

Q: My flight was delayed overnight and the airline didn't provide a hotel. Can I expense one?
A: Yes. Book the nearest reasonable hotel within the normal nightly limit, and note the delay in your expense report.

Q: Can I expense a taxi home from the airport late at night?
A: Yes. Taxis and ride-hailing to and from the airport are reimbursed whenever you are traveling on business, at any hour.

Q: I'm attending a conference that includes breakfast and lunch. What can I claim?
A: Only dinner, up to the daily limit minus the value of included meals. As a rule of thumb, use $15 for an included breakfast and $25 for an included lunch, so in most cities you could claim up to $45 for dinner.

Q: Can I bring my partner on a business trip?
A: Yes, as long as the company pays nothing extra. Hotel rooms for two at the same price are fine; any extra cost, including a larger room, flights and meals for your partner, is yours.

Q: I lost a receipt for a $40 dinner. What do I do?
A: Submit the expense with a signed missing-receipt explanation. Remember that you can do this at most three times per calendar year.

Q: My hotel is $310 a night in Chicago because of a large convention. Is that allowed?
A: Chicago is not a high-cost city, so the limit is $250. If nothing reasonable is available under the limit, book the closest option and add a note explaining the convention. Your manager will review the exception.

Q: Can I use the corporate card for a personal purchase and pay it back?
A: No. The corporate card is for business expenses only. Personal charges, even if repaid, are a policy violation.

Q: Are tips for food delivery covered when I'm working late at the office?
A: Meals while working late at your home office are not covered by this policy. Some teams have separate budgets for late-night work; ask your manager.

Q: I want to take the train instead of flying between two cities. Is that OK?
A: Yes, if the train fare is no more than the economy airfare plus the cost of getting to and from the airport. First-class train travel is allowed when the train trip is longer than 4 hours.

Q: Who approves expenses for a vice president?
A: The chief financial officer approves expenses for vice presidents and above.

Q: How are foreign currency expenses handled?
A: Enter the amount in the currency you paid, and the expense system converts it using the exchange rate on the date of the expense. If your card charged a foreign transaction fee, you may claim the fee as a separate line.


Section 2: Special kinds of travel

Team offsites. An offsite is a gathering of eight or more employees away from a company office for planning, training or team building. Offsites need approval from the department's vice president at least 60 days before the event, using the offsite request form in the travel tool. The request must list the purpose, the number of attendees, the venue, and an estimated budget. The workplace events team books venues and group hotel blocks for offsites; individual attendees should not book their own rooms unless the events team tells them to. Shared activities such as a guided hike or a cooking class are allowed when they are part of the agenda and cost no more than $100 per person. Offsites may not be held at resorts whose main attraction is a casino, golf course or spa.

Candidate and new-hire travel. Recruiting books all travel for job candidates through the travel tool, using the same class of service and hotel limits that apply to employees. Candidates are reimbursed through the recruiting team, not through the expense system, and do not need to follow the receipts section of this policy beyond providing receipts for hotels and transportation. New hires traveling for their first week of onboarding follow this policy in full; their manager approves the trip.

Travel to company offices. Employees who work remotely and travel to a company office for team weeks or planning sessions follow this policy in full. Each remote employee has an annual office travel allowance of $3,000, tracked by the travel tool, which covers flights, hotels and ground transportation for trips to company offices. Trips beyond the allowance need director approval. Remote employees who live within 100 miles of the office they are visiting may claim mileage but not a hotel, unless the visit lasts more than two consecutive days.

Customer visits and field work. Employees who visit customer sites should check the customer's own visitor rules before the trip, including safety training, dress codes and badge requirements. Safety equipment that a customer requires, such as steel-toed boots or high-visibility vests, may be expensed once per year up to $150 in total if the company does not already supply it. Gifts to customers must follow the gifts section below.

Conferences and training. Conference registration fees are booked through the learning team, who can often get group or early rates. Speakers at a conference should ask whether the organizer covers travel before booking, and must not claim any expense the organizer has already paid. Training courses that require travel need the same approval as conferences. If an employee leaves the company within six months of a training course that cost more than $2,500, they may be asked to repay part of the course fee, as described in the education assistance policy.

Section 3: Gifts, entertainment and hospitality

Gifts to clients and partners. Gifts to people outside the company may not exceed $75 in value per recipient per year, and cash or cash-like gifts, such as gift cards, are never allowed. Gifts to government officials, including employees of public universities and state-owned companies, are not allowed without prior written approval from the legal team. Record every gift in the expense report with the recipient's name, company and the business reason.

Gifts received. Employees may accept gifts of modest value, up to $75 per year from any one company, such as a book, a box of chocolates or a branded item. Larger gifts should be politely declined or reported to the legal team, who will decide whether to return them or donate them. Meals and event tickets offered by vendors who are currently bidding for company business must be declined.

Entertainment. Taking clients to an event, such as a sports game or a concert, is allowed when a company employee attends with them and there is a real business purpose. Tickets must be booked at standard prices; premium boxes and resale tickets above face value need approval from the department's vice president. Entertainment with no business purpose, and any entertainment at venues that would embarrass the company, is never reimbursed.

Hosting visitors. When clients or partners visit a company office, reasonable costs of hosting them, such as a lunch in the office or a team dinner, are allowed. Use the client meals rules in the main policy, and list the visitors in the expense report.

Section 4: How expenses are reviewed

Approval chain. Every expense report goes first to your manager. Reports with a single expense over $2,500, or a total over $7,500, also go to your director. Reports from directors go to their vice president. Approvers should review reports within five business days; reports waiting longer than ten business days are escalated automatically to the approver's manager.

What approvers check. Approvers confirm that the trip was approved in advance, that the expenses match the trip dates and destination, that limits in this policy were followed or an explanation was added, and that receipts are attached. Approvers are responsible for the reports they approve; approving a report without reviewing it is itself a policy violation.

Audits. The finance team audits a random sample of about 5 percent of expense reports every month, plus every report that the expense system flags, for example duplicate receipts, weekend expenses on weekday trips, or meals claimed on days with a conference meal. If an audit finds an expense that should not have been reimbursed, the employee is asked to repay it. Repayment is deducted from the next paycheck if not made within 30 days of the request, with the employee's written consent where the law requires it.

Reimbursement timing. Approved expenses are paid by direct deposit in the next weekly reimbursement run, usually within five to seven business days of final approval. Corporate card charges are paid to the card company directly and do not appear in the reimbursement run.

Personal tax. In some cases, such as long-term assignments away from your home office, travel expenses can be taxable to the employee. The payroll team will contact you if a trip may have tax consequences. Do not try to work this out yourself; ask the payroll team.

Section 5: Long-term assignments and relocation

Assignments longer than 30 days. Trips to a single location for more than 30 days are treated as temporary assignments. Instead of hotels, the travel team will arrange a furnished apartment, and a monthly allowance for meals and incidentals replaces the meals rules in this policy. Employees on a temporary assignment may fly home once every four weeks at company expense, or have a family member visit instead. Temporary assignments need approval from the department's vice president and the human resources team, because of possible tax and immigration effects.

Relocation. Moves to a new home city at the company's request are covered by the separate relocation policy, not by this one. Do not use the expense system for relocation costs.

Section 6: Sustainability

The company aims to reduce emissions from business travel by 20 percent over three years. To support that goal: choose a video call when a trip is not clearly needed; choose a train over a flight when the trip by train is under four hours; combine trips to the same region where practical; and choose a direct flight when the price difference is small, since takeoffs and landings use the most fuel. The travel tool shows the estimated emissions for each flight option. Managers are asked to discuss travel plans with their teams each quarter to look for trips that could be replaced or combined.

Section 7: Travel safety and support

Before you go. Read the destination information page in the travel tool, which lists local emergency numbers, travel advisories, and the nearest company office, if any. Save the travel assistance service in your phone; it is available 24 hours a day and can help with lost passports, rebooking during disruptions, finding a doctor, and evacuation in a crisis.

During the trip. If your travel plans change, update the itinerary in the travel tool so the security team knows where you are. If you are in a location affected by a natural disaster, civil unrest or another emergency, the security team will contact you through the travel tool's app; please respond as soon as you can, even if only to say you are safe.

Lost or stolen items. Report a lost or stolen company laptop or phone to the IT help desk right away, wherever you are. Lost personal items are not reimbursed, as noted in the main policy. A lost passport should be reported to the travel assistance service, which will help with the replacement process; reasonable costs of replacing it while on business travel are reimbursed.

Personal safety. Never feel pressured to continue a trip if you feel unsafe. You may change hotels, take a taxi instead of transit, or return home early for safety reasons, and the extra cost will be reimbursed with a short note in the expense report. Employees who face harassment or threats while traveling should contact the security team or human resources; they will be supported.

Section 8: Definitions

Business travel: travel away from your home office of more than 50 miles, or overnight, for company business. Home office: the company office you are assigned to, or your home if you are a remote employee. High-cost city: a city listed in the appendix to this policy. Trip: the period from leaving home or your home office until returning. Receipt: an itemized record from the vendor showing the date, the amount, and what was bought; a card statement alone is not a receipt. Approver: the person who must approve an expense report, as described in Section 4.

Section 9: Changes to this policy

The finance team reviews this policy every year and may update it at any time. Changes are announced in the company newsletter and posted on the finance team's intranet page at least 30 days before they take effect, except for changes that reduce costs for employees, which take effect immediately. Questions about this policy should be sent to the travel and expense channel or to your finance partner.

Section 10: Using the travel tool

Creating a trip. Start every trip by creating a trip request in the travel tool, with the destination, dates and business purpose. Your manager's approval is recorded on the request, and any flights, hotels and cars you book are attached to it automatically. Bookings made outside the tool are not covered by the duty-of-care program and can't be tracked by the security team, so they need a short explanation in the expense report.

Profiles. Keep your traveler profile up to date, including your name exactly as it appears on your passport, your frequent flyer and hotel loyalty numbers, and your seat and meal preferences. The travel tool fills these in on every booking. Your profile is visible only to you, the travel agency, and the security team during an emergency.

Agency help. The travel agency behind the travel tool can be reached by chat in the tool at any hour, for changes, cancellations and complicated itineraries with several stops. Agent-assisted bookings carry a $25 service fee, which is reimbursed; online bookings carry no fee, so book online when you can.

Unused tickets. When you cancel a nonrefundable flight, the travel tool keeps the credit on your profile and offers it the next time you book the same airline. Credits usually expire one year after the original booking. The travel team reviews unused credits every quarter and may ask you to use one on your next trip.

Section 11: Expense categories

Choose the category that best describes each expense, because the finance team uses the categories for budgets and tax reporting. Airfare: flights, seat selection and checked bags. Lodging: hotels and short-term rentals booked through the tool. Ground transportation: taxis, ride-hailing, trains, buses, rental cars, fuel for rental cars, parking and tolls. Mileage: personal car use, entered as a distance, not an amount. Meals while traveling: your own meals. Client meals: meals with people outside the company, with attendees listed. Team meals: meals with only company employees, which need your director's approval unless they are part of an approved offsite. Communications: wifi and phone roaming. Fees: visa, passport photo and foreign transaction fees. Gifts: gifts to people outside the company, recorded as described in Section 3. Other: anything that doesn't fit, with an explanation.

Splitting an expense. If one receipt covers both business and personal costs, such as a hotel bill with a personal room service charge, enter the full amount and then mark the personal part as personal. The expense system subtracts it automatically.

Section 12: More frequently asked questions

Q: I'm traveling with a colleague. Who pays for a shared taxi?
A: Either of you may pay and claim the whole fare. Note the other person's name in the expense report so the fare isn't claimed twice.

Q: Can I book a short-term rental apartment instead of a hotel?
A: Yes, if it is booked through the travel tool and costs no more than a hotel would. Rentals booked directly with a host are not covered by the duty-of-care program.

Q: My checked bag was delayed and I had to buy clothes for a meeting. Is that covered?
A: Reasonable essentials, such as a shirt and toiletries, are reimbursed up to $150 when your bag is delayed more than 24 hours on a business trip, after subtracting anything the airline pays you. Keep the airline's delay report with your receipts.

Q: Can I upgrade my rental car if the company only has a full-size car available?
A: Yes. If the rental company gives you a larger car because nothing smaller is available, that is not a personal upgrade. Add a note to the expense report.

Q: Do I need approval to attend a free webinar or a local meetup?
A: No travel approval is needed for events that don't involve travel or spending. Normal time-off and scheduling rules still apply.

Q: My visa application was rejected. Is the fee reimbursed?
A: Yes, visa fees for business trips are reimbursed whether or not the visa is granted, as long as the trip was approved.

Q: Can I claim a coffee I bought at the airport?
A: Yes, as part of your meals for that day. Coffee and snacks count toward the daily meal limit, not as separate expenses.

Q: I paid a hotel deposit with my personal card. When do I claim it?
A: Claim it after the stay, together with the final hotel bill, so that both appear on the same receipt and the deposit isn't claimed twice.

Section 13: Roles and responsibilities

Travelers. Read this policy before you book, plan trips early, choose reasonable options, keep receipts, and submit accurate expense reports. You are responsible for what you claim, even when someone else, such as an assistant, prepares the report for you.

Managers. Approve trips only when they are needed for the business, consider whether a video call would do, and review expense reports carefully and promptly. Managers are also responsible for making sure new team members know about this policy in their first month.

Directors and vice presidents. Approve the exceptions this policy assigns to you, watch travel spending against your department's budget, and set an example by following the policy yourselves. Department travel budgets are set each year during the planning process and reviewed each quarter.

Finance team. Maintain this policy, answer questions, run audits, process reimbursements, and report travel spending to department leaders each quarter. The finance team also negotiates the company's rates with airlines, hotel chains and rental car companies; booking through the travel tool is what makes those rates available.

Travel agency and security team. The agency books and changes travel and supports travelers around the clock. The security team monitors travel advisories, contacts travelers during emergencies, and approves trips to higher-risk destinations as described in the main policy.

Exceptions. Any exception to this policy that is not described in it needs approval from the chief financial officer in advance. Exceptions approved after the fact are rare and are reported to the audit committee each year.

Section 14: Acknowledgment

Every employee confirms in the learning system, once a year, that they have read this policy. New employees confirm it during onboarding. Contractors who travel on company business confirm it before their first trip, and their agency agreement may set additional limits; if the agency agreement and this policy differ, the stricter rule applies.

THE LIGHTHOUSE AT GULL POINT (Chapter One)

The ferry dropped Mara Quinlan at Gull Point on the last Tuesday of September, along with two crates of tinned peaches, a box of lamp wicks, and a cat she had not intended to bring. The cat, a one-eyed tabby the ferryman called Admiral, had walked aboard at the mainland dock, inspected her luggage, and decided that he was coming too. By the time the island rose out of the fog, Mara had given up arguing with him.

She was twenty-six, and she had never been to sea for longer than an afternoon. The job notice had asked for "a steady person, good with numbers, not afraid of solitude," and the interview had lasted eleven minutes. The lighthouse board had been desperate, she suspected later. The previous keeper, an old man named Elias Brandt, had left in August without giving notice, and the light had been tended since then by a fisherman who rowed over each evening and rowed back each morning, complaining all the way.

The lighthouse itself was a white tower of eighty-two steps, with a keeper's cottage attached at the base by a short covered passage. The cottage had two rooms, a woodstove, a kitchen table scarred with knife marks, and a bookshelf holding nothing but almanacs and a single novel with its last chapter torn out. On the wall beside the door hung a brass barometer that read "Change" no matter what the weather did.

The fisherman, whose name was Tobias Reyes, showed her the routine that first evening. The lamp had to be lit thirty minutes before sunset. The clockwork that turned the lens had to be wound every four hours through the night, by turning a crank exactly forty times. The log had to be written at midnight and at dawn: weather, visibility, ships sighted, and anything unusual. "Brandt was particular about the log," Tobias said. "Particular about everything, really. He'd write down the color of the sea."

"Why did he leave?" Mara asked.

Tobias shrugged in a way that was not really a shrug. "Said he'd heard the bell."

There was no bell at Gull Point. There had been one, a fog bell on an iron frame at the edge of the cliff, but it had been taken down eleven years earlier when the board installed an electric horn. The frame was still there, rusted orange, its crossbar empty.

Mara spent the first week learning the work. She burned her fingers on the lamp glass twice, wound the clockwork forty times at ten, two, and six, and filled the log in a neat, slanted hand. Admiral took up residence on the warm stones beside the woodstove and left only to patrol the rocks at low tide, returning with his paws wet and his opinion of the island unchanged. The supply boat came on Fridays. She learned to ask for more coffee than she thought she would need.

On the eighth night, a little after two, she was winding the clockwork when she heard it: a single low note, rolling in from the sea. It was not the horn, which sounded high and flat. This was deeper, like a bell struck once and allowed to ring until it faded. She stopped with the crank in her hand and counted. Thirty seconds of silence. Then the note again.

She went out onto the gallery. The fog had come in thick, and the beam of the light swept through it like a slow white arm. Below her, the rusted frame stood at the cliff's edge, empty. The sound came a third time, and she was almost certain it came from the water, somewhere to the northeast, where the chart showed nothing but the Hollins Shoal and, beyond it, open sea.

At midnight she had written "Fog, visibility poor, no ships." At three she opened the log again and, after a long hesitation, added: "Heard a bell. Three strokes, thirty seconds apart, from the northeast. Source unknown." Then she sat with the pen in her hand and looked at what she had written, and felt foolish, and did not cross it out.

In the morning she searched the cottage for Brandt's old logs. She found them in a tin trunk under the bed, twenty-three years of them, bound in green cloth. The last volume ended on August 14. In it, in a cramped and careful hand, Brandt had recorded the weather, the visibility, and the color of the sea ("pewter," "bottle green," "the gray of a wet slate") every day for months. Then, starting in June, there were new entries. "Bell, two strokes, NE." "Bell, three strokes, NE, fog." "Bell again. Thirty seconds apart, always thirty." The entries grew more frequent through July. The last one, on August 14, said only: "Seven strokes. I know what it is now. I am going to see."

Under it, someone else had written in pencil, in a different hand: "Light tended by T. Reyes from 15 Aug."

Mara closed the book and sat for a long time at the scarred table. Admiral jumped onto the bench beside her and pushed his head against her arm. Outside, the fog was lifting, and for the first time since she had arrived she could see the Hollins Shoal: a line of white water a mile out, where the sea broke over rocks just below the surface. Beyond it, nothing at all.

When the supply boat came that Friday, she asked the boatman whether anyone had seen Elias Brandt since August.

"Brandt?" He frowned, hauling a sack of flour onto the dock. "Took his dory out on the fourteenth, they say. Calm night. Dory came back on the tide two days later, empty, oars shipped neat as you like." He set the sack down. "Nobody's said it out loud. But nobody's looking for him, either."

That night, Mara lit the lamp thirty minutes before sunset, wound the clockwork at ten, and sat on the gallery with a blanket and a mug of coffee and Admiral in her lap, and waited. The sea was calm and the sky was clear, full of stars. At a quarter to two, the bell rang once.

She did not go down to the gallery rail that night. She sat very still, with Admiral's weight in her lap and the coffee going cold in her hands, and counted. Thirty seconds. A second stroke, low and long. Thirty seconds. A third. Then nothing more, though she waited until the clockwork needed winding again at six and her legs had gone stiff with cold.

At dawn she wrote in the log: "Clear, calm, visibility excellent. Bell, three strokes, NE, 01:45. No fog." She underlined "No fog" twice, because it seemed important, though she could not have said why.

That afternoon she rowed out in the station's little skiff as far as she dared, which was not very far, and looked at the Hollins Shoal from closer up. The sea ran smooth and heavy over the rocks, breaking white only where the swell lifted. There was no buoy, no wreck, nothing that could ring. On the way back she noticed a rope tied off on one of the iron rings set into the landing steps, a newish rope, frayed at the cut end, as though something had been tied there and then cut loose in a hurry.

Tobias came over on Sunday with a string of mackerel and stayed for coffee. She showed him Brandt's last log. He read the final entry twice and set the book down very gently, as if it might break.

"He asked me once," Tobias said, "whether I knew how many men were on the Corrigan when she went down."

"The Corrigan?"

"A schooner. Struck the Hollins Shoal in a fog, sixty-some years ago, before the light was built. That's why they built it." He turned his mug slowly on the table. "Seven men. My grandfather used to say they rang the ship's bell all the way down, so the village would know where to look."

Mara looked at the log, at the cramped careful hand. Seven strokes. I know what it is now.

"Did they find them?" she asked. "The men from the Corrigan?"

"Found the bell," Tobias said. "Not the men. The bell hung on that iron frame up on the cliff for fifty years, until the board put in the horn. Then somebody from the mainland came and took it away for a museum." He finished his coffee. "Or that's what they said."

After he left, Mara climbed the eighty-two steps and stood a long time in the lamp room, looking northeast. When she came down she found Admiral sitting on Brandt's trunk, staring at the wall, his one eye unblinking, and she understood that she was going to row out to the shoal on the next calm night, and that nothing anyone could say would stop her.


But the next calm night did not come for a long time.

The weather turned on Monday. It came in from the southwest in the afternoon, first as a long greasy swell that made the landing steps disappear and reappear, then as rain, then as a wind that leaned on the tower all night and made the lamp room hum like a struck glass. Mara lit the lamp early, because the light had gone strange and brown by four o'clock, and she wound the clockwork at ten and at two and at six with her shoulder braced against the wall. Twice in the night the horn's motor coughed and stopped, and twice she went down into the engine shed with a lantern and a spanner and Brandt's handwritten instructions, pinned to the wall in a sleeve of oilcloth, and coaxed it back to life. The instructions were the most cheerful thing she had read of his. "Tap the governor smartly," they said. "She sulks, but she comes round."

The storm lasted three days. There was no bell in it, or if there was, she could not hear it over the wind. She did not know whether she was relieved.

She slept in pieces, two hours at a time, between windings. In the daytime she read the almanacs, because there was nothing else, and learned the times of the tides for a year that had already passed. She read the novel with the torn-out last chapter, which turned out to be about a sea captain's widow who ran a boarding house, and she found that she minded very much not knowing how it ended. Admiral would not go out. He sat on the windowsill with his back to the room and watched the rain run down the glass, and every so often he made a small, offended noise in his throat, as if the weather were a personal insult that he intended to take up with someone.

On the second day she found the dory's place.

It was in the boathouse below the cottage, a low stone shed at the head of the slipway, where the station's skiff lived on a wooden cradle. She had been inside it only once, on her first day, to see the skiff. Now, looking for a dry place to hang her oilskins, she noticed a second cradle along the back wall, longer than the first, empty, with a coil of rope and a pair of rowlocks hung neatly on a nail above it. Chalked on the beam overhead, in letters she now knew well, was one word: DORY. Beneath the cradle someone had swept the floor clean, and the broom stood in the corner with its bristles worn down to a slant on one side, the way a broom wears when the same hand has used it for twenty years.

She stood there a long while, listening to the rain on the slates. Then she checked the skiff. Its oars were sound, its bung was in, and the little anchor and its line were stowed under the thwart. She took the skiff's lantern up to the cottage, trimmed the wick, filled it, and set it by the door, and did not ask herself what she was doing.
