The storm blew itself out on Thursday morning. The sea stayed big all day, gray and heaving, with the Hollins Shoal breaking white and furious a mile out, the spray standing up off it like smoke. Mara watched it from the gallery with Brandt's binoculars and tried to imagine a small boat out there in that, and could not. Whatever she was going to do, it would not be soon.

The supply boat came on Friday, a day late because of the weather. The boatman's name was Pell; she had learned that much on her second visit. He was a square, slow man who unloaded crates as if each of them had personally disappointed him. This time, along with the coffee and the flour and a sack of potatoes, he handed her a bundle of letters tied with string: the board's monthly circular, a seed catalog addressed to Brandt, and a letter from her sister on the mainland, which she put in her pocket to read later.

"You'll want to write the board," Pell said. "About the horn. They'll send a man out to see to the motor, if you tell them it's been stopping."

"How do you know it's been stopping?"

"Heard it from the village. Stops and starts, they said. Folk notice." He looked at her for a moment. "Folk notice the light too. Regular as a clock, since you came. Brandt's last year it wasn't always."

She wanted to ask him what he meant, but he was already hauling the last crate up the steps, and when he came back down he talked only about the price of diesel. As he was casting off she called after him, on an impulse she did not examine, "The museum. The one that took the bell. Do you know where it is?"

Pell held the boat against the steps with one hand on the iron ring. "Maritime museum in Kestrel Harbor," he said. "Two hours down the coast on the bus. My cousin's girl took her schoolchildren there once." He frowned. "Don't know that they've got a bell, mind. She didn't say."

That evening she wrote two letters at the scarred table, by the light of the lamp. The first was to the lighthouse board, reporting the horn motor and asking politely for the man to be sent. It was easy. The second was to the curator of the maritime museum in Kestrel Harbor, and it took her most of the night, between windings, and three sheets of paper. In the end she kept it short. She was the new keeper at Gull Point, she wrote. She understood that the old fog bell from the station had been given to the museum some years ago. She would be grateful to know whether it was still in the collection, whether it was on display, and whether there was any record of where it had come from before it was hung on the cliff. She did not mention Brandt. She did not mention what she had heard. She signed it with her full name and the name of the station, and addressed it care of the supply boat, which was the only way post came or went.

Her sister's letter she read last, sitting on the gallery in the cold with the beam sweeping over her head. It was full of ordinary things: a new job, a broken boiler, their mother's opinions about both. At the end her sister had written, "Are you lonely out there? You can say if you are." Mara read that line several times. Then she folded the letter carefully and put it inside the cover of the logbook, and found that she was smiling, and could not have explained why.

Tobias came over on Sunday as usual. He brought a jar of his wife's plum jam this time, and a newspaper only four days old, and he admired the way she had kept the horn going through the storm. He had heard it stopping too, he said, and had stood at his window in the village counting the seconds until it started again. She showed him the boathouse, and the empty cradle, and the word chalked on the beam. He looked at it for a long time without saying anything.

"I want to go out to the shoal," she said. "On a calm night. When it rings."

"No," Tobias said at once. Then, more gently: "No. Listen. The shoal is not a place for a skiff at night. The tide sets across it hard on the ebb, and there are rocks out there that only show at dead low water. Brandt knew every one of them, and he still didn't come back." He put down his mug. "Whatever is out there, it has waited sixty years. It can wait for daylight."

"It doesn't ring in daylight."

"Then maybe," he said, "it doesn't want to be found."

They sat without speaking for a while. Admiral, who disapproved of silence when there was jam on the table, climbed onto the bench and sat between them like a small, damp magistrate.

"If you go," Tobias said at last, not looking at her, "you go on the flood, not the ebb. You keep the light on your left shoulder going out, so you stay north of the worst of it. You take the anchor and you don't go closer than the edge of the white water. And you tell me first, so I know to look." He stood up and took his cap from the hook. "And I'll say again that you shouldn't go at all, so that when your sister asks me, I can tell her I said it."

"How do you know I have a sister?"

He nodded at the letter tucked inside the logbook, its envelope showing. "Same handwriting as yours," he said. "Only rounder." And he went down to his boat.

On Monday she went up to the bell frame.

She had walked past it every day, on her way to the woodpile and back, without ever going close. It stood on a shelf of bare rock at the very edge of the cliff, two iron posts and a crossbar, all of it rusted to the color of dried blood and scabbed with orange flakes that came away on her fingers. The bolts that had once held the bell's yoke were still there, sheared off flush with the crossbar. Somebody had cut them with a saw, not unscrewed them; she could see the bright, ragged edges where the blade had gone through, already dulling. The wind came up the cliff face and sang very faintly in the hollow of the crossbar, a thin note, nothing like a bell.

At the foot of the left post, wedged into a crack in the rock where the rain could not reach it, she found a coil of tarred line, old and stiff, and a wooden mallet with a leather-wrapped head. The leather was dark with handling. She turned the mallet over in her hands and thought of the fog nights, fifty years of them, and of a keeper standing out here in the wet with the horn not yet invented, striking the bell by hand, once every thirty seconds, so the boats would know where the rocks were. She put the mallet back exactly where she had found it.

Then, because she could not help it, she went down to the landing steps and looked again at the newish rope tied to the iron ring, the one with the frayed and cut end. She carried the coil of line from the boathouse wall down to compare. It was the same rope: the same weight, the same three strands, the same blue tracer twisted through one of them. Someone had tied the dory to the ring, she thought, and someone had cut it loose in a hurry, and it had not been the sea.

She did not write that in the log. Some things, she was beginning to understand, did not belong in the log. She wrote "Wind light, westerly, sea moderate, visibility good," and the color of the water, which was the green of an old bottle, and she went to bed early, and for once she slept through until the alarm for the two o'clock winding.

On Tuesday the board's circular informed her, in two closely printed pages, that keepers were reminded to economize on lamp oil, that a new pattern of storm lantern would be issued in the spring, and that the annual inspection of Gull Point would take place in November. There was a paragraph near the end, under the heading "Personnel," that said the board regretted to record that Mr. E. Brandt, keeper at Gull Point for twenty-three years, had left the service in August, and that the board thanked him for his long and faithful work. It did not say where he had gone. It did not say anything else at all.

The calm came on the following Wednesday.

It came slowly, as if the sea were tired. The swell dropped through the afternoon until the landing steps stood clear and dry, and by evening the water around the island was so flat that the gulls sitting on it left long trails behind them when they paddled. The sky cleared to the color of a pewter plate, then darkened. A thin moon came up late. Mara looked at the tide table she had copied out of the almanac and worked out, twice, that the flood would begin a little after one in the morning.

In the late afternoon she did the ordinary things, slowly and carefully, as if the ordinary things were a kind of rope she could hold on to. She split a basket of kindling and stacked it by the stove. She cleaned the lamp glass and trimmed the wicks, and polished the brass of the clockwork case until she could see her own face in it, small and pale and serious. She fed Admiral the last of Tobias's mackerel, and he ate it with the air of a creature who had been expecting better. She wrote a short note to her sister and left it, sealed, on the scarred table, propped against the sugar tin where anyone coming in would see it, and then felt ashamed of how dramatic that was, and did not move it.

She lit the lamp thirty minutes before sunset, as she always did. She wrote the midnight entry in the log: "Clear, calm, visibility excellent, light airs from the north. No ships." She wound the clockwork at ten, and then she went down to the boathouse with the lantern, untied the skiff, and walked it down the slipway on its rollers until its bow touched the water. She put the anchor in, and the oars, and the lantern, and her oilskin, though she did not think she would need it. Then she climbed back up to the cottage, because it was not yet time, and because she had promised Tobias.

On the gallery she lit the signal lantern, the one with the red glass, and hung it on the rail facing the village, the way he had shown her. A minute later, across the water, a small yellow light appeared in a window and stayed lit.

She sat down to wait, with the blanket around her shoulders. Admiral did not come to her lap. He sat at the top of the stairs, the stairs down to the cottage and the boathouse and the skiff, with his one eye fixed on the dark, and his tail wrapped tight around his feet.

At a quarter to two, as she was rising to wind the clockwork, the bell rang. One stroke, low and long, rolling in from the northeast across the flat black water.

Mara wound the crank, every turn of it, with her hands steady and her heart going hard. She closed the clockwork case. Then she picked up the lantern, and as she turned toward the stairs, she saw something she had never seen before. Out on the Hollins Shoal, where there was nothing but rocks and moving water, there was a light. A small one, low down, yellow and unsteady, like a lantern held in someone's hand.

The bell rang a second time. Admiral got up from the top of the stairs and went down ahead of her, into the dark, without looking back.

budget.title: City budget memo
budget.text:
MEMORANDUM

To: Members of the Lakeview City Council
From: Office of the City Manager
Subject: Proposed operating budget for the coming fiscal year

Summary. The proposed general fund budget for the coming fiscal year is $84.6 million, an increase of 3.8 percent over the current year's adopted budget of $81.5 million. The increase is driven mainly by negotiated wage increases, higher health insurance premiums, and the full-year cost of the new fire station that opened in March. The budget is balanced without raising the property tax rate, which stays at $1.92 per $1,000 of assessed value. It uses $1.2 million from reserves for one-time expenses, leaving the general fund reserve at 17 percent of expenditures, above the council's policy minimum of 15 percent.

Revenue. Property tax is projected at $38.9 million, up 4.1 percent, almost entirely from new construction and rising assessed values; the rate is unchanged. Sales tax is projected at $21.3 million, up only 1.5 percent, reflecting slower retail activity downtown. Utility taxes are projected at $9.8 million. Fees and charges for services, including recreation programs and permits, are projected at $7.4 million. State-shared revenue is $4.0 million. Other revenue, including fines and interest, is $2.0 million. The remaining $1.2 million comes from reserves, as noted above.

Personnel. Salaries and benefits make up 71 percent of general fund spending. The budget includes a 3.5 percent cost-of-living increase for all employees under the agreements with the police and firefighter associations and the general employees' union. Health insurance premiums rise 9 percent. The budget adds 6.5 new full-time positions: four firefighters to fully staff the new station, one building inspector to reduce permit wait times, one parks maintenance worker, and a half-time grants coordinator. It eliminates two vacant positions in the finance department after the new billing system is automated.

Public safety. The police department budget is $24.1 million, up 2.9 percent. It includes replacing 8 patrol vehicles on the regular schedule and a new records management system shared with two neighboring cities, which reduces our cost by about $180,000 compared with buying our own. The fire department budget is $18.7 million, up 8.2 percent, mainly from the full year of operating Station 4. Average emergency response time citywide fell from 7 minutes 40 seconds to 6 minutes 10 seconds after Station 4 opened.

Parks and recreation. The parks budget is $6.2 million. It restores Sunday hours at the community pool, which were cut three years ago, at a cost of $95,000. It funds the summer youth employment program for 40 teenagers, up from 25. It increases recreation program fees by an average of 4 percent, with a scholarship fund of $60,000 so that low-income families pay no more than before.

Streets and infrastructure. The general fund contributes $3.4 million to the streets program, which, combined with state gas tax and the transportation levy, funds resurfacing of about 11 lane-miles. The city's pavement condition index is 68 out of 100; the council's goal is 72 within five years, which would require about $1.1 million per year more than this budget provides. Staff recommends discussing a possible renewal and increase of the transportation levy, which expires in two years.

Library. The library budget is $2.9 million, flat with the current year. Weekend hours remain unchanged. The budget includes $120,000 for new digital collections, offset by fewer physical periodical subscriptions.

One-time expenses from reserves. The $1.2 million from reserves funds: replacement of the council chamber audio and video system ($310,000), the first phase of an update to the city's comprehensive plan ($450,000), a pilot of electric vehicles for the parks fleet ($260,000), and the city's share of a regional homelessness outreach program for one year ($180,000).

Risks. Sales tax could come in lower if the downtown slowdown continues; each 1 percent shortfall is about $213,000. Health insurance premiums are set by the regional pool and could rise more than projected. The state legislature is considering a change to state-shared revenue formulas that could reduce our share by up to $600,000 starting next year. The budget does not assume any federal grants that have not yet been awarded.

Options the council may consider. If the council wishes to reach the pavement goal sooner, it could shift the $260,000 electric vehicle pilot to streets, or ask voters for a larger transportation levy. If the council wishes to reduce the use of reserves, the comprehensive plan update could be spread over two years, reducing this year's one-time spending by $225,000. Restoring Saturday hours at the branch library would cost about $140,000 per year.

Schedule. The council will hold a public hearing on the proposed budget on November 12, a second hearing on November 26, and is scheduled to adopt the budget on December 10. Department directors will present their budgets in study sessions on October 22 and October 29.

Attachment A: Department budget comparison (general fund, in millions of dollars)

Police: current year $23.4, proposed $24.1, change +2.9 percent.
Fire: current year $17.3, proposed $18.7, change +8.2 percent.
Parks and recreation: current year $5.9, proposed $6.2, change +5.1 percent.
Library: current year $2.9, proposed $2.9, change 0 percent.
Streets (general fund share): current year $3.3, proposed $3.4, change +3.0 percent.
Community development and permits: current year $4.6, proposed $4.9, change +6.5 percent.
Finance and administration: current year $7.8, proposed $7.6, change -2.6 percent.
City council, city manager and city clerk: current year $2.1, proposed $2.2, change +4.8 percent.
Information technology: current year $3.4, proposed $3.6, change +5.9 percent.
Non-departmental, including insurance and debt service: current year $11.0, proposed $11.0, change 0 percent.

Attachment B: Fee changes proposed for the coming year

Building permit fees increase by 5 percent to recover the cost of the new building inspector. Swimming lessons increase from $68 to $72 per session for residents and from $88 to $94 for non-residents. Picnic shelter reservations increase from $45 to $50 per half day. Youth sports league fees are unchanged. Late fees on library materials remain eliminated, as adopted two years ago; the library reports that returns of overdue items rose after late fees ended. Parking at City Hall remains free for visitors for the first two hours.

Attachment C: Community survey results

In this year's community survey of 1,150 residents, the top priorities for city spending were street maintenance (61 percent rated it very important), public safety response times (58 percent), parks and trails (44 percent), and affordable housing programs (41 percent). Satisfaction with street conditions was the lowest of any service, at 38 percent satisfied or very satisfied, compared with 79 percent satisfied with fire and emergency services and 74 percent satisfied with the library. Asked whether they would support a larger transportation levy to repair streets faster, 52 percent said yes, 31 percent no, and 17 percent were unsure. Support was highest among residents who had lived in the city more than ten years.

Attachment D: Staffing summary

Total general fund positions in the proposed budget: 412.5 full-time equivalents, compared with 408.0 in the current year. Six and a half positions are added and two are removed, for a net increase of 4.5. Turnover in the current year was 9.4 percent, down from 12.1 percent the year before, which the human resources department attributes in part to the new hiring bonuses for firefighters and police officers.


Attachment E: Utility funds (not part of the general fund)

The water, sewer and stormwater utilities are run as separate enterprise funds. They are paid for by utility rates, not taxes, and their budgets are presented here for information because they affect residents' monthly bills.

Water. The water fund budget is $14.8 million, up 4.4 percent. The increase pays for the second year of replacing aging cast-iron water mains, about 2.5 miles per year, and for higher costs of the treatment chemicals the city buys from its regional supplier. The proposed water rate increase is 4 percent, which adds about $2.10 per month to a typical single-family bill. Water loss from leaks in the system, which was 14 percent of water produced five years ago, is now 9 percent, and the main replacement program aims to bring it below 7 percent.

Sewer. The sewer fund budget is $11.6 million, up 3.1 percent. The city's share of the regional treatment plant upgrade is the largest cost driver; the plant upgrade is required by the state discharge permit renewed last year. The proposed sewer rate increase is 3 percent, about $1.65 per month for a typical home.

Stormwater. The stormwater fund budget is $3.2 million, up 6.0 percent, mainly to clean and repair culverts after last winter's flooding on the east side. The stormwater fee rises by $0.75 per month per home. Staff will present a stormwater master plan to the council next spring, which is expected to recommend a larger fee increase in future years to address flooding in the lower creek basin.

Combined effect. For a typical single-family home, the combined monthly utility bill rises by about $4.50, or about 3.9 percent. Low-income seniors and residents with disabilities who qualify for the utility discount program continue to receive a 40 percent discount on the base charges. About 1,100 households are enrolled; staff estimates that another 600 may qualify and will mail enrollment information with the January bills.

Attachment F: Capital improvement program, first year

The capital improvement program is a six-year plan for buildings, streets, parks and utilities, presented to the council separately each spring. The first year of the current plan includes the following projects funded by sources other than the general fund operating budget.

Streets: resurfacing of about 11 lane-miles, described in the main memo; safety improvements at the three intersections with the most injury crashes over the last five years; and new sidewalks on the school walking routes near the two elementary schools on the north side, funded mainly by a state safe-routes grant.

Parks: replacement of the 25-year-old playground at Hillcrest Park; resurfacing of the tennis and pickleball courts at Lakeside Park; and the first phase of the riverside trail extension, which will connect the downtown trail to the regional trail system once the second phase is built. The trail project is funded by the parks impact fee paid by new development and a regional grant.

Facilities: a new roof for the public works operations building; energy efficiency upgrades to City Hall's heating and cooling, expected to cut its energy costs by about 20 percent; and design of a replacement for the 1960s-era police evidence building, with construction to be considered in a later year.

Utilities: water main replacement described in Attachment E; replacement of two sewer lift stations; and culvert repairs on the east side.

Attachment G: Five-year general fund forecast

Staff prepares a five-year forecast each year to show whether today's decisions can be sustained. The forecast assumes the current property tax rate, property tax growth of 3.5 percent per year, sales tax growth of 2 percent per year, wage increases in line with recent agreements, and health premiums rising 7 percent per year after this year's 9 percent.

Under those assumptions, the general fund is balanced next year and the year after. In the third year, spending is projected to exceed recurring revenue by about $1.4 million, rising to about $2.9 million in the fifth year, mainly because personnel costs grow faster than revenue. The forecast does not include the possible loss of state-shared revenue described in the Risks section, which would make the gap appear a year sooner.

Staff recommends that the council plan for this gap now rather than wait. Options include reviewing fees for full cost recovery, phasing in the remaining comprehensive plan work, working with neighboring cities to share more services in the way the police records system is shared, and the transportation levy discussion described in the main memo, which would move some street costs out of the general fund. Staff will bring a long-range financial strategy to the council in the spring.

Attachment H: Reserve policy and history

The council's policy requires a general fund reserve of at least 15 percent of expenditures, to protect city services in a recession or emergency. Reserves above 15 percent may be used for one-time expenses, but not for ongoing costs such as salaries. The policy also sets a target of 20 percent, which the city reached before the last recession.

Reserve history. Five years ago the reserve was 21 percent. It fell to 14 percent during the recession, briefly below the policy minimum, and the council approved a two-year plan to rebuild it. It has since recovered to 19 percent at the end of the last fiscal year. Using $1.2 million for one-time expenses this year, as proposed, brings it to 17 percent. The city's credit rating agencies have noted the reserve level and the council's reserve policy as strengths in their most recent reviews, which helps keep borrowing costs low for capital projects.

Attachment I: Performance measures

Each department reports a small set of measures to show what the budget buys. Selected measures for the current year, with targets for the coming year:

Fire and emergency services: responses within 8 minutes, 88 percent this year, target 90 percent. Fire inspections of commercial buildings completed on schedule, 76 percent this year, target 85 percent.

Police: average response time to the highest-priority calls, 5 minutes 20 seconds this year, target under 6 minutes. Share of residents who feel safe walking in their neighborhood at night, 71 percent in the community survey, target 75 percent.

Permits: median time to issue a residential building permit, 34 business days this year, target 20 business days with the new inspector. Share of inspections completed the day after they are requested, 62 percent this year, target 85 percent.

Parks and recreation: recreation program participants, 18,400 this year, target 19,000. Share of park users rating parks clean and well maintained, 81 percent, target 85 percent.

Library: visits, 312,000 this year, target 320,000. Digital checkouts, 146,000 this year, target 165,000 with the new digital collections.

Streets: potholes repaired within 72 hours of a report, 83 percent this year, target 90 percent. Pavement condition, described in the main memo.

Customer service: share of calls to City Hall answered within one minute, 79 percent this year, target 85 percent. Share of online service requests closed within the promised time, 88 percent this year, target 90 percent.

Attachment J: Responses to council questions from the October 22 study session

Question: Why does the information technology budget increase 5.9 percent when the finance department is cutting positions? Response: The increase pays for software subscriptions that replaced older systems, including the new billing system, and for cybersecurity monitoring recommended by the city's insurer. The finance department savings are possible because of that new software. Over the next three years, the combined cost of finance and information technology is expected to be lower than it would have been without the new system.

Question: How many applications does the city receive for the summer youth employment program? Response: Last summer the city received 141 applications for 25 positions. The expansion to 40 positions will still leave many applicants without a spot; staff is talking with local businesses about a matching program for next summer.

Question: Is the regional homelessness outreach program showing results? Response: In its first six months, outreach workers contacted 214 people in the region, of whom 38 moved into shelter or housing. Staff will report again with a full year of data before the city decides whether to continue its share beyond this year.

Question: What happens to the electric vehicle pilot vehicles if the pilot ends? Response: The vehicles would remain in the parks fleet for their normal service life. The pilot is designed to measure fuel and maintenance savings, charging needs, and staff feedback, so that future vehicle replacements can be planned.

Question: Could the city hire the half-time grants coordinator as a contractor instead? Response: Yes, though the cost would be similar. Staff recommends a city position because grant applications often require several years of reporting after an award, and a consistent point of contact makes the city more competitive.

Attachment K: Glossary

General fund: the city's main operating fund, which pays for most services that are not paid for by a specific fee, such as police, fire, parks and the library. Enterprise fund: a fund for a service paid for by its users, such as water. Assessed value: the value the county assessor places on a property for tax purposes, which may differ from its market value. Reserve: money the city keeps for emergencies and one-time needs. Full-time equivalent: a measure of staffing in which one full-time position equals 1.0 and a half-time position equals 0.5. Levy: a voter-approved property tax for a specific purpose and period, separate from the regular property tax. One-time expense: a cost that does not recur in future years, such as equipment or a study.

Attachment L: Changes since the preliminary budget

The preliminary budget shared with the council in September has changed in four ways. First, the regional health insurance pool set its final premium increase at 9 percent, lower than the 11 percent staff had assumed, which reduced costs by about $310,000. Second, the county assessor's final assessed values came in slightly higher than the preliminary estimate, adding about $140,000 in property tax revenue at the same rate. Third, staff added the scholarship fund for recreation programs at the council's request. Fourth, staff removed a proposed new position in the city clerk's office after the clerk found that the new records software would cover the workload. Together these changes reduced the planned use of reserves by about $380,000 compared with the preliminary budget.

Attachment M: Community development and housing

The community development department budget is $4.9 million, up 6.5 percent. Besides the new building inspector, it includes the second year of the online permit system, which now handles 78 percent of permit applications, up from 40 percent before the system launched. Permit applicants can now book inspections online and receive inspection results the same day.

The housing program is funded mainly by federal and state grants that pass through the city, so it appears only in part in the general fund. In the coming year it is expected to fund repairs to about 45 owner-occupied homes for low-income households, mostly roofs, furnaces and accessibility changes, and rental assistance for about 120 households through the county housing authority. The general fund contributes $210,000 to the program's staffing.

Staff is also preparing changes to the zoning code to allow more types of housing near the downtown transit center, as directed by the council last spring. The changes will come to the planning commission in the winter and to the council afterward. They are not expected to affect the budget this year, but over time new housing near downtown would add to property tax revenue and support downtown businesses, which could help the slow sales tax picture described in the main memo.

Attachment N: Downtown sales tax trends

Sales tax from the downtown business district has fallen in five of the last eight quarters, while sales tax from the rest of the city has grown modestly. Staff attributes the downtown decline to the closure of two large retailers, the growth of online shopping, and fewer office workers downtown since more employers began allowing remote work. Restaurants and personal services downtown have done better than retail.

Online sales delivered to addresses in the city now generate about 18 percent of the city's sales tax, up from 9 percent five years ago, because the state requires online sellers to collect tax based on where the item is delivered. This has partly offset the downtown decline.

The economic development office is working with the downtown business association on three projects this year: a program to fill vacant storefronts with short-term pop-up businesses, improved wayfinding signs between the transit center and the main shopping streets, and a series of evening events in the summer. These are funded within the existing economic development budget.

Attachment O: How residents can take part

Residents may comment on the proposed budget at either public hearing listed in the Schedule section, in person or by video. Written comments may be submitted through the budget page on the city's website at any time before the council votes, and every written comment received is shared with all council members. The full proposed budget document, including line-item detail for every department, is available on the city's website and at the main library and branch library reference desks. A plain-language summary is available in English and Spanish. Staff will also hold an informal budget open house at the main library in the week before the first hearing, where residents can ask questions of department directors.

Attachment P: Debt

The general fund pays about $3.1 million a year in debt service, included in the non-departmental line in Attachment A. The largest items are the bonds that built Station 4, which will be paid off in 20 years, and the bonds for the City Hall renovation, which will be paid off in 6 years. When the City Hall bonds are retired, about $900,000 a year will become available for other purposes, and staff recommends that the council decide in advance how to use it, for example for the street program or for the future police evidence building. The city has no variable-rate debt, and its outstanding general obligation debt is about 31 percent of the legal limit set by state law. The city's credit ratings were affirmed this year at the second-highest level from both rating agencies that rate the city. No new borrowing is proposed in this budget.

Attachment Q: Grants

The city applied for nine grants in the current year and was awarded five, worth about $2.4 million in total, mostly for the safe-routes sidewalks, the riverside trail, and the housing repair program. Four applications are still pending, including a federal grant for the east-side culverts. As stated in the Risks section, the budget does not count any grant that has not been awarded; if the pending grants come through, staff will bring budget amendments to the council during the year. The half-time grants coordinator is expected to increase the number of applications the city can submit each year, especially for smaller grants that departments have not had time to pursue.

postmortem.title: Incident postmortem
postmortem.text:
INCIDENT POSTMORTEM: Checkout outage (severity 1)

Summary. For 47 minutes on a Saturday afternoon, between 14:12 and 14:59 UTC, about 64 percent of checkout attempts on the web store and the mobile app failed with an error. An estimated 3,900 orders were lost or delayed, about $286,000 in sales at our average order value. The cause was a configuration change to the payment service's database connection pool, combined with a traffic spike from a promotional email. No customer data was lost or exposed. This postmortem is blameless: its purpose is to understand what happened and prevent it from happening again.

Timeline (all times UTC).
13:05 An engineer on the payments team deploys a configuration change that reduces the payment service's maximum database connections per instance from 50 to 20. The change is part of a planned effort to stay under the database's overall connection limit before adding new services. It passes review; the reviewer approves it on the basis that average connection use per instance is about 12.
13:30 The marketing team sends the weekend promotional email to 1.2 million subscribers, as scheduled. The payments team is not aware of the send.
14:05 Checkout traffic rises to about 3.4 times the normal Saturday level.
14:12 Payment service instances begin to exhaust their connection pools. Requests wait for a connection and time out after 5 seconds. Checkout error rate rises from 0.3 percent to 64 percent within three minutes.
14:14 The error-rate alert fires and pages the on-call engineer for the checkout team.
14:21 The on-call engineer acknowledges the page. The delay was because the alert went to the checkout team's rotation, and the on-call engineer was driving. Checkout dashboards show errors coming from calls to the payment service.
14:29 The checkout on-call engineer escalates to the payments on-call engineer. Payments on-call joins at 14:33.
14:38 Payments on-call identifies connection pool exhaustion in the logs. The team considers scaling out the payment service, but more instances would not help because each instance has the same small pool, and adding instances risks exceeding the database's connection limit.
14:46 The team decides to roll back the configuration change. The rollback requires a full deploy because connection pool settings are read only at startup.
14:55 The rollback deploy completes on all instances.
14:59 Error rate returns to normal. The incident is declared resolved at 15:10 after monitoring.

Root cause. The configuration change reduced each instance's connection pool to 20. Average use was about 12, but peak use under heavy traffic is much higher, and the review did not consider peak load. When the promotional email drove traffic to 3.4 times normal, instances needed about 35 connections each at peak. Requests waited for connections, timed out, and failed.

Contributing factors. First, there was no load test for the configuration change, because configuration changes are not covered by the load-testing requirement that applies to code changes. Second, the payments team had no visibility into the marketing send schedule. Third, the alert paged the checkout team, not the payments team, because errors were measured at checkout, which added about 15 minutes before the right people were involved. Fourth, the connection pool size could not be changed without a restart, which made the rollback slower.

What went well. The error-rate alert fired within two minutes of the start. Once the right engineers were involved, finding the cause took about five minutes. The rollback worked the first time. Customer support posted a banner on the store within 20 minutes of the first page, which reduced duplicate order attempts.

Action items.
1. Require a load test or a documented peak-usage analysis for configuration changes that affect capacity, such as pool sizes, timeouts and rate limits. Owner: platform team. Due in 30 days.
2. Add the marketing send calendar to the engineering on-call calendar, with an automatic notice to service owners 24 hours before any send over 500,000 recipients. Owner: marketing operations. Due in 14 days.
3. Add an alert on payment service connection pool saturation above 80 percent that pages the payments team directly. Owner: payments team. Due in 7 days.
4. Make connection pool size adjustable at runtime without a restart. Owner: payments team. Due in 60 days.
5. Ask a second database expert to review the plan to reduce connection limits, and set per-service pool sizes based on measured peak usage plus 50 percent headroom. Owner: database team. Due in 30 days.
6. Review on-call expectations for engineers who are driving or otherwise unable to respond within 5 minutes, and add a secondary on-call for weekends. Owner: engineering managers. Due in 21 days.

Customer follow-up. Customers who saw a checkout error during the incident window will receive a 15 percent discount code by email, valid for 14 days. Orders that were charged but not confirmed, 112 in total, have been reconciled; each customer was contacted and either the order was completed or the charge refunded.

Lessons. Small configuration changes can have large effects at peak. Our safeguards were designed around code changes, not configuration. Teams that depend on each other need to share schedules that drive load.

Appendix: Detailed metrics

Checkout error rate peaked at 71 percent at 14:31 UTC. Payment service p99 latency rose from 420 milliseconds to the 5-second timeout. Database CPU stayed below 55 percent throughout, which confirmed that the database itself was healthy and the bottleneck was the connection pools. Total connections across all payment service instances peaked at 480, the new maximum of 24 instances times 20 connections, while the database's overall limit is 1,500 connections shared by all services. Before the change, the same traffic would have used about 840 connections across the payment service.

Mobile app checkout failures were slightly lower than web, at 58 percent, because the app retries once automatically after a timeout. Web checkout does not retry. Of the 3,900 failed or delayed orders, about 1,450 customers completed their purchase later the same day, so the estimated net lost revenue is closer to $180,000. The support team received 640 contacts about checkout problems on the day, compared with about 40 on a typical Saturday.

Discussion: why didn't we catch this in staging? The staging environment runs four payment service instances and receives synthetic traffic at about 5 percent of production. At that level, connection use per instance never exceeds 8, so the reduced pool looked safe. Staging load tests exist but run only on code deployments that touch the checkout path. The team discussed whether to run a weekly peak-load test in staging, but staging's database is too small to model production's limits accurately. Action item 1 addresses this through peak-usage analysis instead.

Discussion: why was the rollback slow? Pool settings are read at startup, so a rollback is a full deploy of 24 instances, which our deploy system does in batches of 4 with health checks, taking about 9 minutes. The team considered restarting instances manually but decided the batched deploy was safer. Action item 4 makes pool size adjustable at runtime.

Follow-up review. The incident commander will review progress on all action items at the operations review four weeks after the incident, and the payments team will present the runtime-adjustable pool design at the architecture review before implementation.


Appendix: Incident roles

The checkout on-call engineer served as incident commander from the first page until 14:40, when the role was handed to the payments engineering manager, who joined the incident call at 14:36. A customer support lead served as communications lead, posting the store banner and the status page updates and keeping the support team informed. A second payments engineer joined at 14:41 and served as scribe, keeping the timeline in the incident channel, which is the main source for the timeline in this document. Six other engineers joined the incident channel to help; two of them were asked to step back, because too many people were proposing changes at once in the same thread. The incident process review (see "Process observations" below) addresses this.

Appendix: Customer communications

14:32 The store banner reads: "Some customers are having trouble checking out. We're working on it. Please don't place your order again if you've already been charged." This banner went up 18 minutes after the first page.
14:35 The status page is updated to "Degraded performance: checkout."
14:50 The status page is updated: "We've found the cause and are deploying a fix."
15:02 The status page is updated: "Checkout is working normally. We're monitoring." The store banner is changed to: "Checkout is working again. If you saw an error earlier, you'll receive an email from us."
15:10 The status page incident is marked resolved.
Next day, 10:00 The customer email with the discount code is sent to customers who saw a checkout error.

Social media mentions of the store rose to about 900 in the hour of the incident, compared with about 60 in a normal Saturday afternoon hour. The social media team replied to the most-shared posts with a link to the status page. Several customers praised the banner's advice about not placing duplicate orders.

Appendix: Five whys

Why did checkouts fail? Because the payment service timed out waiting for database connections.
Why were there no connections available? Because each instance's pool had been reduced below what it needed at peak traffic.
Why was the pool reduced below peak need? Because the change was sized on average usage, and nobody involved in the change looked at peak usage.
Why did nobody look at peak usage? Because our review checklist for configuration changes doesn't ask for it, and configuration changes are exempt from the load-testing requirement.
Why are configuration changes exempt? Because the load-testing requirement was written three years ago after an incident caused by a code change, and at the time capacity settings were rarely changed. Since then, more of our capacity has been controlled by configuration, but the requirement was never revisited.

The team agreed that the last answer is the most important one: our safeguards had not kept up with how we actually change the system. This is the reasoning behind action item 1.

Appendix: Database connection budget

The production database allows 1,500 connections in total, shared by every service that uses it. At the time of the incident, peak connection use by service over the previous 30 days, excluding the payment service, was: orders service 310, inventory service 190, accounts service 140, promotions service 95, reporting jobs 120, and administrative tools 30, for a total of 885. The planned new services, a gift registry and a subscription service, are expected to need about 150 connections between them at peak. This was the reason for the original effort to reduce the payment service's share. With 50 percent headroom on measured peaks, as action item 5 proposes, the total demand would exceed the database's limit, so the database team is also evaluating a connection proxy, which lets many service connections share a smaller number of database connections. The proxy evaluation is tracked separately and is not a condition for closing this incident's action items.

Appendix: Related incidents

Eight months ago, the search service had a 20-minute partial outage after a change to its request timeout setting, also a configuration change, also deployed without a load test. That postmortem recommended reviewing all capacity-related settings across services, but the recommendation had no owner and was not completed. This incident is the second in a year caused by an untested capacity setting. Action item 1 is intended to close that gap for good, and the engineering leadership team has agreed to review open action items from all severity 1 and 2 postmortems every month, so that recommendations without owners don't get lost again.

Two years ago, a marketing email sent during a database maintenance window caused a slowdown in the account sign-in service. That postmortem recommended sharing the marketing calendar with engineering, which was done for a few months through a shared document that was later forgotten. Action item 2 makes the notice automatic rather than relying on people to check a document.

Appendix: Detection and alerting review

The checkout error-rate alert worked well: it fired within two minutes of the start of the incident. The problem was routing. The alert measured errors at checkout and paged the checkout team, who had to work out that the errors came from the payment service and then find the right people. The payment service had its own latency alert, which also fired at 14:13, but it was configured as a warning that posts to the payments team's chat channel rather than paging anyone, and no one was watching the channel on a Saturday afternoon.

The team reviewed all alerts for the checkout path and found three more cases where a downstream service's problem would first be detected by an upstream alert that pages a different team. Each of those will be changed so that both teams are paged when the upstream alert fires and the downstream service's latency or errors are also above their thresholds. The alert on connection pool saturation in action item 3 will be added to all services that use the shared database, not only the payment service, at the database team's recommendation.

Appendix: Process observations

The incident channel was busy and at times confusing: about 340 messages in 50 minutes, with several parallel discussions. Two people proposed scaling out the payment service at the same time as payments on-call was reading the logs, and the scale-out was nearly started before the incident commander stopped it. The team recommends that only the incident commander approve changes to production during an incident, and that people who join the channel to help post in a separate thread unless asked to speak in the main one. These are already part of the written incident process, but the process had not been practiced recently; the engineering managers will run an incident drill each quarter starting next month.

Handing off the incident commander role from the checkout on-call to the payments engineering manager went smoothly and should be the norm when the cause turns out to be in another team's service.

Appendix: Marketing send process

Marketing operations sends about eight large promotional emails a month, most of them on weekends. Until this incident, engineering learned about large sends only when traffic rose. The marketing team has agreed to the automatic notice in action item 2, and also to two further changes: large sends will be split into batches over 30 to 60 minutes rather than sent all at once, which spreads the traffic spike; and the marketing team will check the engineering change calendar before scheduling a send, so that sends do not coincide with planned risky changes. A send of more than 1 million recipients will require a short check-in with the on-call engineers of the checkout and payments teams on the day of the send.

Appendix: What we decided not to do

The team discussed and decided against several other changes. Freezing all configuration changes on weekends was rejected because some urgent configuration changes, such as blocking abusive traffic, must happen on weekends, and a freeze would push risky changes to busier weekdays instead. Adding automatic retries to web checkout, as the mobile app does, was deferred: retries helped the app during this incident, but retries during a capacity problem can also make it worse by adding load, and the checkout team wants to design retry limits carefully first. Raising the database's overall connection limit was rejected by the database team because the database's memory is sized for the current limit.

Appendix: Action item tracking

Each action item has a ticket in the reliability project, linked from this document, and its owner reports status in the weekly reliability meeting until it is closed. An action item is closed only when the change is in production and, where it applies, has been tested: for example, the pool saturation alert will be tested by deliberately filling a staging pool and confirming that the page reaches the payments on-call. Action items that slip past their due date are listed at the top of the weekly meeting's agenda.

Appendix: Glossary

Connection pool: a set of open database connections that a service instance keeps ready and reuses for requests, instead of opening a new connection for each one. Pool exhaustion: when every connection in a pool is in use and new requests have to wait. p99 latency: the response time that 99 percent of requests are faster than. Severity 1: our highest incident severity, used when a core customer flow such as checkout is broken for many customers. Blameless postmortem: a review that looks at how systems and processes allowed an incident to happen, rather than who made a mistake. Rollback: undoing a change by deploying the previous version or setting. Incident commander: the person who coordinates the response to an incident and approves changes during it.

Appendix: Impact by channel and region

Web store customers in North America were most affected, because the promotional email went first to the North American list and most of the extra traffic came from there. Checkout failures in Europe were lower, about 41 percent at the peak, because it was evening there and traffic was lighter. Customers paying with saved cards failed at about the same rate as customers entering a new card; the failure happened before the request reached the payment processor, so the payment method made no difference. Gift card redemptions also failed during the window, because they go through the same payment service. Store pickup orders were affected in the same way as delivery orders.

Appendix: Cost of the incident

Besides the lost sales estimated in the detailed metrics, the incident had these direct costs: about 60 hours of support overtime on the day and the following Monday to handle contacts and follow-up emails; the expected cost of the discount codes, estimated by the finance team from past redemption rates at about $41,000 in discounts if redemption matches past apology codes; and processor fees on refunded charges. The finance team estimates the total direct cost, not counting lost sales, at about $55,000. The harder cost to measure is customer trust; the customer insights team will compare repeat purchase rates for affected and unaffected customers over the next 90 days and share the result at the operations review.

Appendix: Peak-usage analysis template

Action item 1 allows a documented peak-usage analysis instead of a load test. The platform team has drafted a short template, to be attached to any capacity-related configuration change. It asks: What setting is changing, and from what value to what value? What is the measured peak usage of this resource over the last 90 days, and on what date and at what traffic level did that peak occur? What traffic level do we expect at the next known peak, such as a sale, a holiday or a large email send? What is the expected usage at that level, and how much headroom remains? What happens to customers if the limit is reached? How can the change be undone, and how long would that take? The reviewer must confirm the numbers by looking at the dashboards, not just read the answers. Changes where the expected usage at the next peak is within 30 percent of the new limit need a load test instead.

Appendix: Runtime-adjustable pool design notes

The payments team has started the design for action item 4. The proposed approach reads the pool's maximum size from the configuration service every 30 seconds and grows or shrinks the pool gradually, by no more than five connections per interval, so a mistaken setting cannot instantly flood the database. Shrinking waits for connections to be returned rather than closing connections in use. Every change is logged with who made it and why. A hard ceiling, set per service by the database team, prevents any service from raising its pool beyond its share of the database's limit without the database team's approval. The design will be presented at the architecture review, as noted in the follow-up review section, before implementation begins.

Appendix: Questions raised at the review meeting

Would canary deployments have caught this? Probably not. Configuration changes go through the same canary step as code, one instance first for ten minutes, but at 13:05 traffic was normal and the canary instance never needed more than 14 connections. A canary only catches problems that show up at the traffic level during the canary period.

Was the original change wrong? The goal was right: the database was approaching its connection limit, and new services were coming. The change was sized on the wrong measure. The engineer who made it and the reviewer both followed the process as it was written. That is why this postmortem focuses on the process.

Could the payment service have failed more gracefully? Yes. When the pool was exhausted, requests waited the full timeout before failing, and customers saw a generic error after a long spinner. The checkout team will add a clearer message, asking customers to try again in a few minutes and reminding them that they will not be charged twice, for cases where the payment service is unavailable. This is a small change and will be done within the regular sprint, without a separate action item.

Should the promotional email have been paused once the incident started? It had already been delivered by the time the incident began, so pausing it was not possible. For future incidents, the marketing team will pause any scheduled sends that have not yet gone out when a severity 1 incident is declared, until the incident commander says it is safe to continue.

Appendix: Document history

Draft written by the payments team in the three days after the incident, from the incident channel, the dashboards and interviews with the people involved. Reviewed at the postmortem meeting with the checkout, payments, database, platform, support and marketing operations teams. This version includes the changes agreed at that meeting, and it will be updated with links to each action item's ticket as they close.

Appendix: The days after the incident

Sunday. The payments team confirmed that every payment service instance was running with the original pool setting and that connection use had returned to its normal pattern. The support team worked through the backlog of contacts, prioritizing customers who reported being charged without receiving a confirmation. The database team began collecting 90 days of peak connection data for every service, which is the input to action item 5.

Monday. The incident was reviewed briefly at the weekly operations meeting, and the postmortem owner and due date were set. The marketing team reviewed its send schedule for the rest of the month and moved one large send from a Saturday afternoon to a Tuesday morning, when engineering staffing is fuller. The platform team started drafting the peak-usage template.

Tuesday and Wednesday. Interviews with the engineers involved, the reviewer, the support lead and the marketing operations manager. Every interview was framed around what each person saw and knew at the time, not what they should have done. Several people mentioned that they had been uneasy about weekend coverage for months but had not raised it formally; this is reflected in action item 6.

Thursday. The postmortem meeting was held and the action items were agreed. The pool saturation alert from action item 3 went into review the same day.

Thanks. The authors thank the support team, who handled more than fifteen times their usual Saturday volume with patience and good humor; the engineers who gave up part of their weekend to join the incident and the follow-up work; and the marketing operations team, who joined the review with open minds and suggested two of the improvements to the send process themselves. Questions about this postmortem can be raised in the reliability channel or at the weekly reliability meeting.

venue.title: Wedding venue guide
venue.text:
THE ORCHARD HOUSE: WEDDING AND EVENT GUIDE

Welcome. Thank you for considering The Orchard House for your celebration. Our property includes a restored 1920s barn, a lawn with mature apple trees, a covered patio, and a bridal cottage. This guide covers pricing, what's included, our policies, and the timeline for planning. Please read it carefully; your contract will refer to it.

Capacity. The barn seats up to 180 guests for a dinner with a dance floor, or 220 for a cocktail-style reception. The lawn ceremony site seats 250. The covered patio holds 80 for cocktails. If your guest count exceeds 180 for a seated dinner, you'll need a tent on the lawn, which we can arrange through our preferred rental company.

Pricing. Saturday rental from May through October is $9,800. Friday and Sunday rental in the same months is $7,200. Rental from November through April is $5,500 on any day. Thursday events are $4,800 year-round. Rental includes the property from 10 a.m. to 11 p.m. on the event day, with music ending at 10:30 p.m. Additional hours, if available, are $600 per hour and must be booked at least 30 days in advance. All prices are before the 9 percent service charge and applicable sales tax.

What's included. Rental includes the barn, lawn, patio and bridal cottage; 20 round tables seating 8 to 10, 2 long farm tables, and 200 white wooden folding chairs; string lights in the barn and over the patio; a sound system for the ceremony with one wireless microphone; on-site parking for 120 cars; a day-of venue coordinator; and setup and breakdown of our own furniture. Linens, dishes, glassware and additional furniture are not included.

Catering. You must use one of our five approved caterers. Each has worked at the property and knows our kitchen and power limits. A list with contact details is in the appendix. Food trucks are allowed for late-night snacks only, with prior approval, and must be from the approved list as well.

Alcohol. You may provide your own beer and wine, but it must be served by a licensed and insured bartending service. Spirits are allowed only if served by a bartending service that holds a liquor license for events. Bar service must end 30 minutes before the end of the event. No shots, and no self-service bars of any kind. Guests under 21 may not be served, and bartenders will check identification.

Deposit and payments. A non-refundable deposit of 50 percent of the rental fee is due at signing to reserve your date. The remaining balance, plus the service charge and a $1,000 refundable damage deposit, is due 60 days before the event. The damage deposit is returned within 14 days after the event, less any charges for damage, excessive cleaning, or violations of this guide.

Cancellation. If you cancel more than 12 months before the event, we'll refund half of your deposit. If you cancel 12 months or less before the event, the deposit is not refundable. If you cancel within 60 days of the event, the full rental fee is owed. If we're able to rebook your date at the same or higher price, we'll refund any amount you paid beyond the original deposit. Date changes are allowed once, at least 9 months before the event, for a $500 fee, subject to availability.

Weather. The ceremony may be held on the lawn or, in bad weather, in the barn. The decision must be made by noon on the event day, in consultation with your coordinator. If you'd like a tent as a backup for the lawn, it must be reserved at least 30 days before the event.

Decorations. You may decorate the barn and lawn with freestanding decorations. Nothing may be nailed, stapled or taped to the barn's walls or beams; you may use the existing hooks. Open flames are allowed only in enclosed glass holders. Confetti, glitter, rice, birdseed and sky lanterns are not permitted anywhere on the property. Bubbles and real flower petals are allowed outdoors. All decorations must be removed by the end of the rental period.

Vendors. All vendors must provide proof of liability insurance at least 30 days before the event. Vendors may arrive no earlier than 10 a.m. and must finish loading out by 11:30 p.m. Bands and DJs must use our power outlets on the barn stage and keep volume under 95 decibels, measured at the back of the barn.

Rehearsal. A one-hour rehearsal is included, scheduled on the day before the event between 3 p.m. and 6 p.m., based on availability. If the property is booked that day, we'll offer another time during the week.

Accommodations. The bridal cottage is available from 10 a.m. on the event day for getting ready; it has two vanities, a full-length mirror, and a small kitchenette. There is no overnight lodging on the property. A list of nearby inns with group rates is in the appendix.

Guest transportation. Because of the narrow road, buses larger than 30 seats cannot reach the property. Shuttle vans are recommended for groups. All guests must leave by 11 p.m., and no vehicles may be left overnight without approval.

Planning timeline. Twelve months out: sign the contract and pay the deposit. Nine months out: book your caterer and bartending service. Six months out: book other vendors and reserve any tent. Ninety days out: send us your vendor list. Sixty days out: pay the remaining balance and damage deposit. Thirty days out: submit vendor insurance, your final timeline, and your floor plan. Fourteen days out: confirm your final guest count. One week out: final walkthrough with your coordinator.

Accessibility. The barn, patio and restrooms are wheelchair accessible. The bridal cottage has two steps at the entrance; a portable ramp is available on request. Accessible parking spaces are next to the barn.

Frequently asked questions

Can we bring our dog? Well-behaved dogs are welcome for the ceremony and photos, on a leash and with a designated handler, and must leave the property before the reception begins. Please tell your coordinator in advance.

Can we have fireworks or a sparkler send-off? Fireworks are not permitted. Sparklers are allowed for a send-off on the gravel drive only, not on the lawn or near the barn, and a bucket of water must be on hand. Your coordinator will supervise.

Is there a backup for power? The barn has a backup generator for lighting and the sound system, but not for catering equipment. Caterers bring their own generators if needed, placed behind the barn.

Can children attend? Yes. Children must be supervised at all times, and the pond at the bottom of the orchard is off limits. We can recommend local childcare services that will set up a kids' room in the cottage after 6 p.m.

Do you have a preferred photographer? We don't require specific photographers, but we keep a list of photographers who know the property and the best spots at different times of day. The orchard is especially popular for photos in the hour before sunset, and in late September the apple trees are in fruit.

Can we have a second event the next day, like a brunch? A next-day brunch is possible on Sundays from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. for $1,800, if the property isn't booked. It includes the patio and lawn but not the barn.

What happens if there's a power outage or another emergency that makes the property unusable? If the property cannot be used because of an event beyond our control, we'll offer you the first available date of your choice within 12 months at no extra charge, or a full refund of everything you've paid, including the deposit.

Do you allow outside desserts? Yes, a wedding cake or dessert from a licensed bakery is allowed even if your caterer doesn't provide it. There is no cake-cutting fee from us, though your caterer may charge one for plating and serving.

Can we have a live band? Yes. Bands must load in through the barn's side door, finish sound checks by 4 p.m. if the ceremony is in the barn, and follow the volume limit. Amplified music is not allowed on the lawn after 7 p.m. out of respect for our neighbors.

How many restrooms are there? The barn has four restrooms, one of which is accessible. For more than 200 guests, we recommend renting a restroom trailer, which can be parked behind the barn.


Appendix: Approved caterers

Each of our approved caterers has cooked in our kitchen many times, knows how far the kitchen is from the barn (about forty paces along a covered path), and understands our power limits. All of them can accommodate common dietary needs, such as vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free and nut-free meals, if you tell them early. Contact details are provided with your contract packet.

Hearth and Vine: seasonal farm-to-table menus served family style or plated; known for wood-fired vegetables and local cheeses; minimum of 60 guests.

Blue Heron Catering: plated dinners and buffets with a strong seafood menu; offers a full late-night snack service; minimum of 75 guests.

Sabor Kitchen: Latin American menus, stations and family-style service; popular for taco and empanada late-night stations; minimum of 50 guests.

Golden Crust Barbecue: smoked meats, sides and a dessert bar, served buffet style; brings its own smoker, which is placed on the gravel pad behind the kitchen; minimum of 80 guests.

Linden and Rye: formal plated service, including multi-course tasting menus; can provide wine pairing advice to your bartending service; minimum of 40 guests.

Appendix: Approved late-night food trucks

Three food trucks are approved for late-night service: a wood-fired pizza truck, a crepe and waffle truck, and a grilled cheese truck. Food trucks park on the gravel pad next to the patio and may serve for up to 90 minutes. They must have their own power or use the outdoor outlet next to the gravel pad, which supports one truck at a time.

Appendix: Nearby lodging

There is no overnight lodging on the property, but several inns nearby offer group rates to Orchard House guests. Group blocks are usually released about 30 days before the event, so we recommend booking yours as soon as your date is set.

The Millbrook Inn: 24 rooms, 3 miles away, a short drive along the river road; offers a breakfast for wedding parties on the morning after.

Fernwood Lodge: 40 rooms and 6 cabins, 7 miles away; has a large lawn and fire pit that many couples use for a welcome gathering the night before.

The Station House Hotel: 60 rooms in a converted rail depot in town, 9 miles away; the best choice for guests without cars, since most of the town's restaurants are within walking distance.

Hollow Creek Bed and Breakfast: 8 rooms, 2 miles away; often booked by the couple's families for the whole weekend.

Several vacation rental houses are also available within 10 miles. We don't manage them and can't vouch for them, but past couples have shared good experiences.

Appendix: Kitchen and power

The catering kitchen has two commercial ovens, a six-burner range, a warming cabinet, two prep tables, a three-compartment sink, a hand sink, an ice machine, and a walk-in cooler. There is no dishwasher; caterers bring their own dish service or use rental dishes that go back dirty. The kitchen's electrical service supports the installed equipment plus up to four additional plug-in warmers. The barn stage has two dedicated circuits for bands and DJs. Other areas, including the patio and lawn, have limited outlets, and extension cords across walkways must be covered with cord protectors, which we provide. Our coordinator will walk your caterer and band through the power plan during the final walkthrough.

Appendix: Ceremony and reception layouts

Lawn ceremony. The ceremony site faces west under the two largest apple trees, with the barn behind the guests. Chairs are set in two sections with a center aisle of about five feet. Our coordinator places the chairs; you choose the number of rows and whether to add a second aisle for very large ceremonies.

Barn ceremony. In bad weather, or by choice, ceremonies can be held in the barn with chairs facing the stage. A barn ceremony needs a room flip of about 60 minutes before dinner, while guests have cocktails on the patio. Your caterer and our coordinator handle the flip together.

Reception. The standard reception layout places round tables on both sides of a central dance floor, with the head table or a sweetheart table in front of the stage. Long farm tables work well for a family-style meal. Your floor plan must keep the two barn exits and the path to the restrooms clear, and must leave at least 36 inches between tables for servers. We have sample floor plans for several guest counts, which your coordinator will share.

Cocktail hour. The covered patio holds cocktail hour for most guest counts. Larger groups can spill out onto the lawn next to the patio, with high-top tables and lawn games. Lawn games are welcome; we keep a set of cornhole boards and a giant Jenga set that you may use at no charge.

Appendix: Photography at The Orchard House

The best light on the lawn is in the hour before sunset, when the sun comes through the apple trees from the west. The barn's big sliding doors frame the sunset nicely for portraits from inside. Other popular spots are the old stone wall at the edge of the orchard, the patio under the string lights after dark, the bridal cottage's porch, and the meadow path down toward the pond, as long as everyone stays on the path and away from the water's edge. In spring, the orchard blossoms for about two weeks, usually in late April or early May. In summer the trees are full and green. In late September and early October, the trees are heavy with fruit; guests may pick an apple or two, but please don't climb the trees or use ladders. Drones are allowed for photography with prior notice, operated by a licensed pilot, and not over guests during the ceremony.

Appendix: The day-of coordinator

Every event has a day-of venue coordinator from our team. Your coordinator is your main contact from 30 days before the event, leads the final walkthrough, and is on the property from the time vendors arrive until the last vendor leaves. On the day, the coordinator opens the property, meets each vendor at arrival, checks that the floor plan is set correctly, cues the ceremony processional with your officiant and musicians, manages the rain decision with you, and enforces the policies in this guide, including timing and volume, so you don't have to. The coordinator is not a wedding planner: they don't design your day, manage your vendors' work, or handle personal items such as gifts and cards. Many couples also hire a planner or a day-of planner of their own, who works alongside our coordinator.

Appendix: Rentals

Linens, dishes, glassware, flatware, and furniture beyond what we provide are not included in the rental. Most of our caterers can arrange them for you; otherwise, our preferred rental company delivers to the property and knows our layout. Rentals may be delivered on the event day after 10 a.m., or on the day before if the property is free; ask your coordinator. All rentals must be picked up by noon on the day after the event, or by the end of the rental period if another event is booked the next day. Rental companies are vendors under this guide and must provide proof of insurance.

Appendix: Parking and getting home safely

On-site parking is on the mown field next to the barn, with attendants recommended for events over 100 guests. Our coordinator can help you arrange parking attendants through our preferred rental company. Ride-hailing service is limited in the area late at night, so we strongly recommend arranging shuttle vans or a local taxi service in advance for the end of the night. Guests who are not able to drive safely may leave their car overnight with approval from the coordinator, as long as it is collected by 10 a.m. the next morning.

Appendix: Smoking

Smoking and vaping are allowed only in the designated area on the gravel drive, away from the barn, the patio and the orchard, where sand buckets are provided. The orchard grass is very dry in late summer, and a single cigarette can start a fire. Smoking anywhere else on the property results in a deduction from the damage deposit.

Appendix: Trash, recycling and sustainability

Your caterer is responsible for removing food waste, and our team handles recycling and the remaining trash from the barn and lawn. We compost the property's green waste and use the compost in the orchard. We encourage couples to choose real dishes over disposables, to donate leftover flowers to local senior centers, and to work with caterers who donate untouched food. Several of our approved caterers partner with a local food rescue group; ask them about it.

Appendix: Neighbors

The Orchard House sits in a farming valley with neighbors on three sides. Our music and volume rules exist because of agreements with those neighbors and the county, and keeping them is a condition of our event permit. Please ask your guests to drive slowly on the narrow road, especially after dark, and not to park on the road shoulder. We appreciate your help in keeping good relations with the people who make it possible for us to host celebrations here.

Appendix: A sample event day

Every wedding is different, but many of our couples follow a day much like this one, for a ceremony at 4:30 p.m. in September.

10:00 a.m. The property opens. Our coordinator meets the rental company and the florist. The couple and their wedding party arrive at the bridal cottage to get ready.
11:00 a.m. The caterer arrives and begins setting up the kitchen. Tables and chairs are placed according to the floor plan.
12:00 p.m. The rain decision: lawn or barn, made with the coordinator.
1:00 p.m. The photographer arrives. The band or DJ arrives and loads in through the barn's side door.
3:00 p.m. Sound checks are finished. First look and wedding party photos in the orchard.
4:00 p.m. Guests begin arriving. The bartending service opens a water and lemonade station near the ceremony site.
4:30 p.m. The ceremony on the lawn.
5:00 p.m. Cocktail hour on the patio. Family photos on the lawn.
6:00 p.m. Guests move into the barn for dinner. Welcome and toasts.
7:15 p.m. Sunset photos for the couple in the orchard while guests finish dinner.
7:45 p.m. First dance, parent dances, and the dance floor opens.
9:00 p.m. Cake cutting. A late-night food truck opens on the gravel pad.
10:00 p.m. Last call at the bar, followed by the end of bar service.
10:30 p.m. Last dance, and the music ends. Sparkler send-off on the gravel drive.
11:00 p.m. Guests have left. Vendors finish loading out.

In September the sun sets around 7:15 p.m., which is why many couples choose a ceremony time between 4 and 5 p.m. Your coordinator will help you adjust the schedule for your date.

Appendix: Ceremony details

You are responsible for your marriage license and for choosing an officiant; check the county's rules on timing and witnesses early. Our sound system for the ceremony includes one wireless microphone, usually worn by the officiant. If you'd like your readers or musicians to have microphones too, your band or DJ can provide more. An arbor made from reclaimed orchard wood is available at no charge, and many couples decorate it with flowers. Aisle runners are allowed on the lawn only if they are weighted, because the wind comes up the valley in the afternoon. Unplugged ceremonies, where guests are asked to put away their phones, are popular here; your coordinator can make the announcement for you.

Appendix: Accessibility details

Besides the accessible barn, patio and restrooms described in the main guide, the path from the parking field to the barn is packed gravel and is wheelchair accessible in dry weather. The lawn ceremony site is reached by a mown path with a gentle slope; in wet weather, golf cart transport is available on request for any guest who needs it. Reserved aisle seating for guests who use wheelchairs can be included in your ceremony layout. The bridal cottage's portable ramp should be requested at least two weeks ahead. If any of your guests has specific access needs, please tell your coordinator, who will plan around them.

Appendix: Seasonal notes

Spring weddings may be cool in the evenings and the lawn can be soft after rain; we recommend a tent backup for April and May. Summer is warm and dry, and the barn's large fans and open doors keep it comfortable; we provide water stations for guests. September brings mild days, cool evenings and the apple harvest, and it is our most popular month, so dates book well over a year ahead. October evenings can be cold; patio heaters can be rented, and many couples add blankets for guests at the ceremony. Winter weddings are held in the barn, which has radiant heat, and the property is decorated with evergreen garlands and white lights from late November.

Appendix: Questions to ask on your tour
